subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he is in a position to inform the house about the results of the discussions held in Washington by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and more particularly whether he can confirm the report in the press that the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that one of the objectives of Canadian policy was to persuade those nations concerned, in this case the United States and the United Kingdom, that there should be no movement from Jordan against Iraq.
Right Hon* J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister): There is really nothing I can tell the house at this time that would be of any assistance. Yesterday, as everyone knows, the Secretary of State for External Affairs discussed the situation at great length with both the British foreign secretary, Mr. Lloyd, and the Secretary of State of the United States, Mr. Dulles. In consequence, following those discussions, he is meeting this morning -I think the meeting is under way now- with Mr. Hammarskjold. What passed yesterday will be brought to Mr. Hammarskjold's attention, to the end that every effort will be made to bring about the amelioration of the very grave situation that prevails at the moment.
57071-3-153
So far as the United Nations is concerned, as you know the present position is that all three resolutions failed of adoption, that is those submitted by the United States, the U.S.S.R. and Sweden. At the conclusion of the sitting the delegate for the United States moved that an emergency session of the United Nations general assembly be called. However, that has not yet been decided upon finally, and the United Nations security council will meet again on Monday.
I think I might add that the endeavour of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on behalf of Canada is to assure that while the matter is still in a state of flux, no step be taken whatsoever which would extend any possible action by any nation beyond the boundaries of Jordan or Lebanon. I think that is as far as I would like to go at this time. I can tell the house that every effort is being made by the Canadian government to make its contribution to the end that the serious situation may be, if not solved, at least greatly diminished in its danger and peril.

There was a question I asked the minister yesterday to which he has not replied. Perhaps he would care to answer it now. It was in connection with the proposal reported to have been made in December at the NATO council meeting and again at the defence ministers' meeting in April in regard to a NATO food pact, and the reference by the United States ambassador when he was before the congressional committee in Washington to the effect that the Canadian government had made no detailed proposals of any kind and that they were waiting to hear from the Canadian government before they could express their views.

A proposal for establishing a food bank has been made on several occasions during the last 12 years. When hon. gentlemen opposite were in power they had this matter under consideration. If there is general agreement among the NATO nations that a food bank should be established, Canada is quite prepared to play her part in that type of development.

That does not quite deal with my question. Would the minister comment on the statement of the United States government that the Canadian government has made no detailed proposal in NATO, and that without receiving further details regarding the Canadian proposal it is impossible to tell how it might fit into NATO planning. I mention this because so much was made of it in the house last autumn after the council meeting in Paris, and also because the Minister of National Defence made a public statement about it after he got back in April.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

If the Leader of the Opposition is referring to something in the nature of a formal presentation to the NATO organization, which I presume he has in mind, my understanding has been that it was discussed informally at that meeting in Paris. Responsibility rests also with other nations in the NATO group, not solely with Canada. The proposal was put forward; if it is not acceptable to other NATO countries it is a little difficult to proceed in the matter. My own understanding is that the matter is still under review, and that ways and means are being considered for the establishment of a food bank which in times of crisis and emergency would certainly be of great assistance to countries that may be in danger.

In view of the fact that Canada has more to gain from this proposal than perhaps any other NATO country, will the government take the initiative in putting this proposal formally before the NATO council as was suggested by the United States ambassador when he was in Washington in the testimony before the committee which I have just mentioned? It is one thing to have informal conversations, as the hon. gentleman knows; it is quite something else to put a formal proposal before the NATO council for inclusion on the agenda of the council for consideration and possible action.

We in this group are exceedingly interested in the whole question of a food bank for NATO countries, or for that matter in an international world food pool as has been suggested in this house from time to time. I think the whole question of a food bank in Europe is one that should be given full support in this house. I remember Lieutenant General Guy Simonds making the statement that if we had a food bank of wheat in Europe instead of the CF-105 the expenditure in his opinion, would have been more worth while.
I am wondering if there has been any discussion among the NATO countries as to whether some of the money Canada now spends on armaments might be transferred to an account for the establishment of such an emergency reserve of food, in the belief that by doing so we would be making a contribution to defence even more adequate than the contribution we are now making.
Certainly we support wholeheartedly the idea of a food reserve for NATO countries. We go one step further and say there should be an international food pool so that people in deficit food producing areas may be saved from the pangs of starvation by getting surpluses from the surplus producing countries where those surpluses, incidentally, cause a great strain on food prices.

Perhaps I could throw a little light on the subject, as I attended the defence ministers' conference in Paris in April, where I made on behalf of the government of Canada the offer and proposal that a food pool should be established in Europe in order that there might be held certain stocks of flour, wheat and other commodities which could be used in the event of an outbreak of hostilities. At that meeting the whole matter was referred to the permanent council. Various questions have been asked since regarding the cost and the method of storing and packaging this material. The whole subject is now being investigated by the permanent group of the NATO.

I wonder if the minister could say when the discussions may reach a point where a decision is likely to be made. I am sure that with such important discussions in progress the minister has some general idea as to when the discussions may terminate, a conclusion be arrived at, and the conclusion either accepted or rejected.
1 could not possibly forecast as to when other people will arrive at a decision in this matter.

Well, Mr. Chairman, the
Minister of National Defence has given us rather different information than that which we secured from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I suggest it might be well for the government, then, to take the matter up with the United States government because of the wrong impression which must have been given-inadvertently, of course-by the United States ambassador to Canada in the hearings before the foreign relations committee of the United States Senate. I quote from those hearings, as I quoted from them yesterday. The ambassador said:
.-the Canadian government has made no detailed proposal in NATO or to the United States government that such a bank be established-
He went on to say that the government of the United States-
-will of course be glad to consider any detailed proposals which may be made in NATO by our Canadian friends.
The Minister of National Defence said that such a detailed proposal has been made, and perhaps it would be desirable to clear this matter up with the United States government and get that government to consider it, because of this indication of its willingness to do so.

Mr. Chairman, possibly I could say a word in this connection. I brought this matter before the NATO council in the month of December as a proposition

that deserved the attention of the nations joined together on behalf of freedom. In so far as an international food bank is concerned, or a food pool, it is obvious that the achievement of such an organization is impossible. It has been considered over and over again at FAO meetings. One who has made a very detailed study of the subject and has made the strongest representations to the FAO is Mr. Hannam, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I received from him the detailed study he had made of the subject, and presented it in a general way to the NATO council in Paris in December.
Was this a formal proposal made to the NATO council by the Prime Minister?

I am coming to that. In the light of subsequent events, I think the stand I took at that time was a reasonable and necessary one to take. I pointed out the fact that the U.S.S.R., while pretending at all times to have no aggressive purposes, was building up a very large submarine fleet. Submarine fleets are not built up for defence. The U.S.S.R. has some 570 submarines whose purpose-this is more than inference on the basis of previous experience with nations which went in for submarine activity-would be in large measure to paralyse food reserves and by bringing about a state of famine achieve indirectly or psychologically what it might not be able to attain militarily.
The suggestion was made knowing that there was no possibility of attaining an international organization and having regard to the fact that FAO, with the tension of the international situation in the last several years and being composed of others in addition to the freedom-loving nations, could not hope to attain any success in this direction. It was brought up on that occasion not in a formal way but as one of those things that deserved consideration and discussion. Nothing was presented in a formal way at that meeting of the 15 heads of the various NATO countries. The discussions were informal, the purpose being an exchange of ideas and ultimately, in consequence of the discussions, the making of fuller representations.
The Minister of National Defence did so, as he has already stated, and it is not for me to enter into any discussion of statements made by ambassadors of friendly countries. But I can say that the matter is under consideration, and I think the events of the last two weeks underline the necessity of action in this regard.
When I brought the matter to the attention of the NATO meeting I pointed out that the establishment of such a food bank was possible, was in my opinion necessary and was
Supply-Trade and Commerce one of those things that might be done under article 2 which for so long received so little attention by the NATO organization. It would achieve two purposes. First, it would remove the overhanging surpluses that today have a detrimental effect on agriculture in general. Second, it would bring about a degree of security in defence in that it would make food supplies available to the countries in Europe which, if left to themselves, would have difficulty in increasing their output of agricultural products to the degree necessary to provide reasonable and proper sustenance in those countries.
Now that most realize that NATO preserved the peace in the last several years and that its defences have been such as to make the countries represented in NATO reasonably secure against the danger of aggression, in my opinion a further step is necessary. Certainly what is happening now gives added emphasis to the need that we do something to assure that if conditions change and defence measures become necessary for survival, a food bank will be available. If war breaks out one can only hope that the merchant fleets will be able to operate. Beyond that one cannot go. Because of that I think what is happening today in the Middle East and the gravity of the world situation will give added emphasis to the need of action in this connection.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the Prime Minister has made an important statement, and we hope that every effort he makes toward the establishment of a food bank among the NATO countries in Europe will meet with success. In addition to having made certain general comments at the meeting of the NATO heads of state as well as the more detailed discussion by the defence minister, I think the Canadian government should consider making a concrete offer to the NATO countries, since without question we are one of the countries that would be called upon to supply a very large part of the food going into any such food bank. Interested as we are in moving surpluses from this country and putting purchasing power into the economy, as well as providing this kind of reserve in case of an emergency whether brought about by conflict of arms or by very bad crops such as France had some time ago, we think this is a good idea.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that it would be an imaginative step on his part, the kind of step that might result in concrete action, if Canada would say to the NATO countries something like this. We have 100 million bushels of wheat that we will put into a NATO food pool now. We are prepared to supply it, and if necessary we are prepared to pay the cost of it now. In

Supply-Trade and Commerce addition, I think Canada should put a price tag on the wheat at a level that would give our wheat producers a reasonable return.
In my opinion that is a very sensible idea. It is time something was done through food pools and other actions to increase the price of wheat or the whole wheat economy of western Canada will suffer further deterioration. Therefore I suggest that the Prime Minister should offer the NATO countries 100 million bushels of wheat at a price of $2 a bushel.
Now, there may be snickers from the occupants of the benches behind the Prime Minister, but I do not believe the $200 million involved is an expenditure we should immediately reject because of its size as being something entirely impossible. There is another way this amount may be provided, and that is to say to the NATO countries: If you feel that such a food pool is important perhaps part of our defence expenditures now made for the purchase of other items could be used for the purchase of such a quantity of grain.
When we are discussing a regional food bank for emergency purposes. I would suggest to the Prime Minister that there are even stronger reasons for providing a food bank for the Colombo plan countries. That is an area where starvation is always close at hand. That is an area where people require the surplus food we have in this country. I feel that Canada should go even farther than she has gone in providing such assistance to Colombo plan countries.
I do not believe the economic strain on the Canadian nation would be on a level that might suggest itself at first sight to people who are not conversant with the grain industry. The Prime Minister knows that many millions of bushels of wheat have been held in storage in this country for four, five or perhaps even six years. The government is now paying very substantial sums towards the cost of storage of this grain, and in these estimates there is over $40 million for that purpose. The worst thing you can do with wheat is to keep it on hand for five or six years. The storage or carrying charges eat up most of the value of the wheat and you have lost it in an economic sense, though you still have the wheat on hand. It would have been much more economic for this country if the former administration had provided by way of gifts, paid for out of the national treasury, substantial quantities of wheat. The cost to the Canadian economy would not have been any greater.
I would suggest to the Prime Minister that in addition to these general discussions, Canada should make some concrete offer, and

we should endeavour to have established in the Colombo plan countries a food pool where it will be needed in the years ahead to combat famine.

I agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia. The house will have heard with great interest and satisfaction, I think, the statement that has been made by the Prime Minister on this matter. He quite rightly divided this subject, the establishment of a food bank, between its international and its NATO aspects. The subject of an international food bank has been before the United Nations food and agriculture organization for many years. The purpose behind this proposal, which has not been carried into effect, has been both economic and humanitarian. In that sense that kind of food bank would serve the purpose which my hon. friend has just mentioned in connection with the Colombo plan countries.
The Colombo plan itself, as my hon. friend knows, was not established as a mechanism for consumer goods assistance but rather for capital and technical assistance. The NATO food bank has both economic and defence aspects. It has economic aspects in that it would strengthen the economies of the North American members of NATO if surplus wheat could be disposed of in part in this way. It would even strengthen the economic position of the European members of NATO by sterilizing, in a financial and economic sense, some of these surpluses so they would not be overhanging the market.
Perhaps more important so far as NATO is concerned is the defence aspect. When I say that I am thinking of defence in its 1958 aspect and not in its 1914 aspect, because in the light of the kind of war to which we would be subjected if war were ever allowed to break out, food would be not only a necessity for defence but a necessity for survival in Europe. We would be deceiving ourselves if we ever thought that, in terms of an atomic war, the Atlantic shipping lanes would be kept open. The only chance the European countries would have of getting food for survival would be the food that would be on the spot at the time.
While this proposal may have been a desirable thing five or ten years ago, it is far more necessary now. It is for that reason we should hope that this proposal, which in some form or other has been made by the Canadian representative to NATO, by the Prime Minister last December and apparently in more detail by the Minister of National Defence in April, will be followed up. This would seem to be the time to do it. I am certain it will get a more constructive and favourable reaction from some of the European members

of NATO now than it received in the earlier days of NATO, when the necessity may not have seemed so great.
I would hope, therefore, that this proposal which has been made will be followed up vigorously. I also hope that perhaps the minister concerned would be able to make a report to this house on the consideration that has been given to it by the permanent council, because the Minister of National Defence said it had been before the permanent council. He went into some detail as to how it could be worked out. There are problems of storage, problems of turnover and other technical problems. If the permanent council has been discussing this subject it will be interesting for the house to have a report on that matter.
Finally, it surely is important, because we cannot do this without the co-operation of the United States and that applies to so many things these days, to remove any impression in Washington which seems to exist in the minds of some members of the executive, and which must have been created in the minds of members of congress by this testimony of May 13, that the Canadian government has not made such a proposal and is not anxious to see the proposal carried into effect.

I find greater support in this house than I did last December at the NATO meeting for the suggestion which I made then for the first time. It was the first occasion that this had been brought to the attention of the NATO organization. As the Leader of the Opposition says, the proposal has two elements in it, that of need and also that of defence. Placing them in reverse order, I am sure the government will be very gratified with the views expressed by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Assiniboia in reference to this matter.
I do not want to make any reference to the evidence given or the testimony furnished to the committee by the ambassador. I might add that recently there was a press report to the effect that the commander of the Atlantic NATO forces felt this plan had merit, and that on the basis of the hypotheses that have been advanced now by the Leader of the Opposition, if war came it would be very difficult to keep open the lanes of commerce, there was a greatly increased and intensified need for action in this direction.
In so far as the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia are concerned in connection with extending this beyond the NATO countries and giving to it a Colombo plan connotation, may I say this. While all of us agree that food is of primary interest, a transcendent necessity if those who oppose communism in

Supply-Trade and Commerce the east are to be able to maintain their stand, I have not at any time since I became Prime Minister had any evidence that the nations within the commonwealth in Asia have that same desire he has expressed to have available to them wheat and other food products in bulk and in large measure. They have made their requests. As a matter of fact, while this government has increased the amount of food available under the Colombo plan it has always found that the viewpoint of the brother nations in Asia is generally that the assistance should be, as was said by the Leader of the Opposition, in technologicial or machine assistance and not food assistance and the like.
Food was accepted in Ceylon. Food was needed because of famine conditions there last fall and in the early winter. With that exception the attitude of the Asiatic nations of the commonwealth has certainly been far removed from that of the hon. member for Assiniboia, who appeared to think that these nations are reaching out and demanding additional food assistance beyond the comparatively small amounts needed to meet immediate and emergency conditions.
However, I want to thank both hon. members for their contributions to this matter. My friend the hon. member for Assiniboia spoke of an imaginative plan. He certainly produced one which was in no way limited by financial considerations. On occasion, Mr. Speaker, I have heard criticism to the effect that we should be extremely careful that we do not overexpend. While I do not take second place to anyone in my desire to achieve some degree of economic assistance to those countries, I realize the limitations imposed not only by financial needs and requirements but also by the wishes of the countries in question.
I sometimes think that if we had given greater attention to economic assistance we might, in the light of events that have taken place since 1943 or 1944, have been able to preserve a higher degree of resistance among certain nations, and in particular China, of which it has been said by Mr. Hoffman that if in 1944 the nations of the free world-then the allied nations-had contributed $400 million by way of economic assistance the events of history might have been otherwise than they have been. However, all of us have far better capacity to judge in the light of events after they have taken place than to say with certainty what is going to take place in the future.
At this particular time when everywhere in the world-and I am speaking of the present moment-there is a tremendously intensified psychological propaganda campaign

Supply-Trade and Commerce on the part of the Soviet and other communist nations, all of us in the free world will have to make a new reassessment of matters such as this. But again I say that it is on occasions such as this that the House of Commons when it gives its undivided attention to a matter for the benefit of the nation, touches its highest point and achieves its greatest opportunity for the people. I thank both hon. gentlemen for their contributions, the Leader of the Opposition for what he has said in the light of his wide and extensive experience in the field of foreign affairs and my friend the hon. member for Assiniboia for his continued interest in this subject.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to the comments of the Prime Minister. As to the cost of the 100 million bushels of wheat that I suggested, I do not think we can say offhand or can say immediately that a $200-million expenditure is one that we would reject outright because of any drain it might make on the national treasury. If the proposal for a food pool in Europe means anything in concrete terms, as I am sure it does, I am certain that it will have to be paid for. I am sure that when Canada made such a suggestion the government must have had in mind-I would expect this to be so-bearing part of the financial burden of such a food pool. If that is the case, any suggestion that it might have been in the neighbourhood of $200 million I think is not at all out of the way.
I was rather disturbed, though, at the minister's remarks on my suggestion of a food pool for Colombo plan nations. We realize that a food pool for Europe is a good deal different from a food pool for Colombo plan countries. A food pool for Europe is not something that is likely to be needed immediately, at least we certainly hope not. Certainly the people in that area do not need the addition of bread grains to their diet. But in the Colombo plan countries I think the situation is entirely different. When the Prime Minister says those countries have never suggested that they should have additional food instead of technological and machine assistance, I think he is right; in fact I know he is right. Even though millions of people in Colombo plan countries are next door to starvation almost every day of their lives, their governments take the attitude that if there is ever to be an improvement in their standard of living they must industrialize; and they will industrialize, if necessary, on the basis of an even lower food intake for their people. It is a question of improving their standard of living for the future no matter what the sacrifice to the present generation.

That is not what I had in mind when I suggested a food pool for Colombo plan countries. I did not have in mind saying to them: We are going to give you $35 million, but we hope that instead of taking it all in technological and machine assistance, you will take $10 million of it in wheat. That is not what I had in mind at all. What I had in mind was something over and beyond what we are now doing; a food pool, a reserve of food which would be available to those countries in time of need.
Another reason those countries are reluctant to take these gifts of food at a given time, which gifts they sometimes feel are more on the basis of getting rid of a surplus by the country making the donation than with a view to meeting their long-term needs, is that it is no solution to the problem of feeding their people who are hungry today if they are going to be allowed to starve tomorrow. In such a way one is just postponing the end. They are interested in establishing some kind of plan whereby they can get regular supplies of food so there might be a general improvement in their diet on a longterm basis.
When I put forward the suggestion of a food pool for Colombo plan countries I am thinking of something in addition to technological and machine assistance. I am thinking in terms of long-range planning which would add to the calorie intake of the people of these areas; and if that kind of proposition were to be put to the governments of the Colombo plan countries I am firmly convinced that they would accept it without reservation or objection.

I want to say just a brief word before the item carries with respect to a subject introduced yesterday by the hon. member for Ottawa West and referred to later by the hon. member for Laurier. I have in mind the matter of the Canadian National Steamships and trade with the West Indies.
I think we on this side of the house were all gratified by what the minister said with respect to the government's intention to provide a ship for interisland trade in the West Indies. That idea, of course, originated when we were in office, and we are naturally flattered that the government should carry it out. The minister, in referring to Canadian National West Indies ships said, I think quite correctly, that at the present time the traffic was being adequately carried by other ships. While we believe that to be true we do know that although the population of Canada increased by 3 per cent last year our export trade increased by only 1 per cent. Our trade is therefore falling behind our rate of development, and we have high hopes that the Federation of the West Indies will

result in a vastly expanded trade, not next year but over the years, between that federation and Canada.
This shipping service of the Canadian National Steamships was, of course, originally undertaken pursuant to the Canada West Indies trade agreement of 1926. The service has been in operation since 1927; and if the government find it quite impossible, as they seem to have decided it is, to get these ships operating under the aegis of the Canadian National Railways-I gather the Minister of Transport has given up hope of doing that-I hope that before the government sell these ships outright so they would have no further connection with Canada, consideration might be given to the possibility of transferring the ships themselves under some mutual aid or lend-lease or some analogy with the Colombo plan to the West Indies. At the same time the West Indies might be given a measure of technical assistance so the service might be operated as it has been operated for 30 years between Canada and the West Indies.
My hon. friend from Gloucester reminded the minister last night about the situation in Saint John, New Brunswick, where there is a threat that the sugar refinery may be closed down and its operations moved to central Canada. I do not know whether it is a valid reason, but one of the reasons given in a public speech by the head of this enterprise for this prospective was that the freight cost to Saint John from the West Indies is almost as high as it is from the West Indies to Montreal, and that sugar shipped from Saint John to central Canada had, of course, to pay in addition the rail freight or an extra ocean freight.
It may be that these ships could continue to be operated on a somewhat different basis, and it may be that the government would even consider it worthwhile to give some financial assistance to their operation. It might be that by operating to Saint John and Halifax and then from either of those ports to St. John's Newfoundland and then direct from St. John's to the West Indies, cargoes could be provided on a triangular basis which would make it possible to cut the freight costs somewhat.
It has, of course, been a grievance for a long time in Newfoundland that the bulk of our fish had to be shipped to Halifax and then transshipped, and as a result the freight on Newfoundland fish is considerably higher than it is on exactly the same fish shipped from Nova Scotia. It happens that from a geographical point of view St. John's is nearer to the West Indies than Halifax, but I would not suggest for one moment that the rate from Newfoundland should be lower than the
57071-3-154
Supply-Trade and Commerce rate from Nova Scotia. It is, however, the desire of everyone in Newfoundland to find some way in which these rates can be equated; and if it were possible, by operating this service from the West Indies on a lend-lease or mutual aid arrangement so that the ultimate title to the ships would remain with Canada although they were completely operated by the West Indies people under their own conditions and by their own arrangements, it might be possible to retain this industry in New Brunswick and to equalize the freight rates on our fisheries products as between Nova Scotia and Newfoundland to the West Indies. It is always possible, of course, to pick up in Halifax or Saint John cargoes of package freight of one kind or another shipped from central Canada to Newfoundland.
I think the Minister of Transport would agree with me that at almost all times there is hanging over the Canadian National a surplus of freight which has to get across Cabot strait; and to have this additional service available to carry freight between Saint John or Halifax and St. John's would ensure cargoes in all three directions. Of course I am not an expert and this is a project which would require a good deal of study. I do not expect the minister to make any comment about it, at this time unless he wishes to do so, but I feel that although the Minister of Transport had the prime responsibility for its operation, since this service was originally instituted for the promotion of trade with the West Indies, and since we are very anxious in the Atlantic provinces to expand that trade as rapidly as possible, that the government should take one more look at this alternative suggestion before we get rid of those ships in such a manner that they will be altogether lost to that service and to Canada.

May I make myself clear? I was not referring to purchases by this department. The Department of Defence Production, in answer to a question I asked some time ago, made a return showing large purchases of automobiles from Germany. It seems to me, and I know it does to many thousands of other people, that it is most unusual for a department of government to buy automobiles made in Germany at a time

when there is so much unemployment in the automobile industry in Canada. In other words, does the minister regard it as within his functions to deal with that kind of problem?

It is certainly not a primary responsibility of the Department of Trade and Commerce, but I can assure my hon. friend of my intense interest in the problem he has raised. From time to time I have mentioned to my colleagues that it is advisable to buy in Canada when that can be done. At the same time, the Department of Trade and Commerce keeps in mind the fact that our exports are dependent upon the purchasing power of importing countries. Trade is a two-way street. Then I would like to draw to the attention of the minister what was said on this subject by the Prime Minister when he was making a very strong attack upon the opposition as recorded on page 3527 of Hansard for January 20, 1958.
That was during the last parliament?

Yes. The minister will see that the Prime Minister, among other things, was making accusations against the former administration. It will be recalled that the house rose on April 12, 1957, and the Prime Minister accused the opposition of not having tabled this document-presumably before April 12-and of not having published it before June 10, 1957. This is the kind of language he used in his accusation:
-for political purposes, having concealed this document-
And:
-have the effrontery to pretend-
And so on. I just want to draw to the attention of the minister the strength and violence of the language used by the Prime Minister in his criticism of the former government for not having published a document prepared in March 1957 prior to June 10. The minister will appreciate that we have now reached July 19 but have still not had this year's document tabled, and I would like to ask him if he does not consider the government should be consistent in this matter?
I do not think the hon. member should look for consistency as between one government and another.
Oh, oh.

I think my question is quite fair. The Prime Minister outlined the policy with respect to the publishing of these documents and he did so in a rather forceful manner. I would think that since we are dealing with the same government the minister should follow the same policy in order to be consistent.
I have some remarks to make, Mr. Chairman, but if the minister wishes to comment on the comment of the hon. member for Ottawa West I would be very glad to wait.
I would be very glad if the hon. gentleman would continue.

On the same point, Mr. Chairman, the minister has made an observation which is rather difficult to understand. He inferred that the hon. member for Ottawa West was speaking of consistency between this government and the preceding government.
The Liberal government.

Yes, and the Liberal government. That clearly shows that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, quite understandably on a Saturday afternoon, has not followed the observations of the hon. member for Ottawa West because that hon. gentleman was not referring to any act which might be considered consistent or inconsistent as between two governments of different political complexions. What he was referring to was the statement made by the man who is now the head of the present government and who was also the head of the government in the month of January last, and the question is as to the inconsistency between the observations of members of two governments of which the same right hon. gentleman was and is the head. That is the question before the Minister of Trade and Commerce and no furrowing of the eyebrows of the minister should suggest that it is a difficult one to follow, because it is not. The fact is, as the hon. member for Ottawa West pointed out, that rising in his place in the month of January last, the present Prime Minister in the course of a speech he was making in answer to a question put by the present Leader of the Opposition accused the previous administration of withholding a report which he later identified as one marked "Private and Confidential". This report, he implied, had it been revealed to the Canadian public would have been responsible for the previous administration receiving at the hands of the people a much more severe form of censure than was, the Prime Minister said, administered to it in the
Supply-Trade and Commerce month of June 1957. The previous government, it was said, had failed to reveal to the Canadian people important facts which they were entitled to have, facts which revealed the state of the economy and developing situation.
We all remember that day in the house when the Prime Minister rose and attacked the Leader of the Opposition and those of us on this side of the house for having withheld this document. He spoke about it for almost an hour. Then he went all over the country stating that the previous administration had withheld from the people of Canada and from parliament a document whose contents they were entitled to know. The Minister of Trade and Commerce well remembers that.
The question now is: why is this present parliament not given the opportunity of knowing the contents of the same report for the present year? If it was right for the present Prime Minister to criticize the previous administration for withholding that document, is it not right for those of us on this side of the house to ask the Prime Minister to treat that document in 1958 in exactly the same way as, in the month of January, he thought the Canadian people and the Canadian parliament should have been treated with regard to it in 1957?
That is the point, and either the Prime Minister was entirely wrong in what he said in January with regard to the economic survey of 1957, or the position now taken by the government is inconsistent with the position the Prime Minister took in regard to that document in January last. Why should the economic survey prepared in the minister's department and paid for out of his estimates not be given to this house now? Can the minister explain that?

I thought that yesterday the Leader of the Opposition and I had buried this report, but apparently not. The Prime Minister will read Hansard with interest with regard to the comments which have been made, and I will convey to him personally some of the emphasis, vigour and emotional fervour that has been put into those comments by hon. gentlemen opposite.
In order to be consistent, I think that in view of the fact that the 1957 report was not made available to the opposition of that time, the 1958 report should, similarly, not be produced at this time.
Oh.

If hon. gentlemen opposite are asking for consistency, the practice followed by the Liberal administration was not to make this report public, and since the opposition is now asking for consistency we take exactly the same stand. In fact, this
2442	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce question has been answered in the house on several occasions by the Prime Minister as well as by myself. This document, and other documents of a similar nature, are confidential departmental paper for the use of officials and ministers in departments. The practice of the former Liberal administration-
Was correct, then.
-was not to make this public, and we are simply following along those lines.

I must not let pass the suggestion of the minister that he and I had agreed last evening that this matter should be buried. He buried it, and I was not able to disinter it at that time. But we have another opportunity, because this is the item in the estimates which covers the publication of reports of this kind. As my hon. friend from Essex East has said, we remember so well that scene on January 20 when the Prime Minister, his voice shaking with party indignation and quivering with contrived emotion, attacked us because we did not produce this report in the spring of 1957. Therefore the remarks the minister has just made are extremely interesting because he has repudiated the attack made by his leader, the Prime Minister. He has accepted our position and agreed that this kind of report should not be made public. He does not intend to make it public in 1958, as we did not make it public in 1957.

Mr. Chairman, there is no repudiation whatsoever of the speech of the Prime Minister. I think he was right. I listened with interest to his remarks last January, and the quivering was all on the other side of the house. I am not at this stage saying that the report will not see the light of day, but I do say it will not be published at this particular moment.

If the minister now says that the Prime Minister was correct when he attacked us last January for not making this report public in the spring of 1957, and if he accepts the Prime Minister's position, then he is wrong in refusing to make this report public at this time. He must be consistent in this matter or repudiate the statement made by his Prime Minister, and I wish he would let us know which line he really intends to follow.
I will clarify the hon. gentleman's mind with regard to the matter. I will continue to support the Prime Minister.

Well, Mr. Chairman, as the Leader of the Opposition has pointed out, far from being buried this question is now being projected forward in


proper perspective. The Leader of the Opposition has asked a perfectly legitimate question in the face of the statements made and the position taken by the Prime Minister in January of this year with regard to the economic survey for 1957. The Minister of Trade and Commerce for whom this report was prepared must tell the house by implication or by words whether the position now taken by the government is the correct position to take or whether the position taken by the Prime Minister in January is the correct position for the government to adopt in this matter. The minister must remember that this economic survey reached him first. It reached him as Minister of Trade and Commerce before it reached any of his colleagues. Presumably he saw this report before the Prime Minister or any other member of the present administration. Did he, when he saw it, or later, bear in mind the words of the present Prime Minister, who is reported at page 3528 of Hansard for 1957-58, volume 4, as having said:
Why did hon. members opposite, in the idealistic vein of the Leader of the Opposition, not reveal these facts?
He was referring to facts which had been gleaned from the report.
Why did they not act on them, even if they did not think fit to reveal them?
Hear, hear.

I am glad hon. members on the government side are applauding that statement.
Why did hon. gentlemen, opposite in the idealistic voice of the Leader of the Opposition not reveal these facts-
And act on them.

The hon. member for Renfrew South said: "Hear, hear". He is one of those who along with so many others heard the present Prime Minister in the election of this very year tell the people that one of the reasons why our party should not be returned was because it had concealed facts to which they were entitled as Canadian citizens.
And now hon. gentlemen reaffirm this. The hon. member for Renfrew South nods his head. Apparently he agrees with me. If that is the case why does he not rise in his place now and ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to do exactly what the Prime Minister asked us to do, reveal these facts?
You did not do it.
They are trained seals now.

If the Minister of Trade and Commerce fails to lay on the table the economic survey of 1958 that is

a clear vindication of the position taken by the previous administration. It shows the extent to which the right hon. gentleman and hon. gentlemen opposite are prepared to go during the course of an election in urging on the people the acceptance of certain positions which within three months of that election they reverse. .
Shame.

That is the situation. The Prime Minister was speaking in the city of Saint John, New Brunswick when he said there that as far as the government of which he is the head is concerned it would take the Canadian people into its confidence on every measure in which it felt it was prudent at the time so to do and that this kind of information was the kind of information about which the previous administration should have advised the Canadian people.
Somersaulting.
Tell the truth.

My hon. friend says, "Tell the truth". Let the truth come out now with respect to this same document. Let us know if there is going to be a continued state of unemployment. Let us know what are the prognostications of the government's advisers for the future. Hon. gentlemen opposite who made a great point on the eve of the last general election in the attack made on my leader will find that in the judgment of the Canadian people the attack was not justified. They will discover that in the minds of the Canadian people the attack was not a fair and valid one in the face of the reluctant and anaemic reply to which this committee has been treated by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Mr. Chairman-
Oh, oh.
Mr. Chairman-
You said that.
Mr. Chairman, I should just like to say one word at this time. I was one of those who took part in the last election and I happen to be one of those who was elected.
That is too bad.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend who just sat down is misconstruing the argument used by at least some of us in the last election. I should like to make it clear that what we condemn was not that the report was not revealed, but the report was made to the cabinet and the cabinet should have acted upon it-at least, I am speaking for myself-
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You had better.

I cannot say what may have been said in other places by other hon. members. But I do not want to be accused by the hon. member for Essex East of being one of those who in the last election condemned the previous government for failing to reveal the report because in my opinion- and it always has been my opinion-it was a report to the cabinet.
You called it a hidden report.

What we condemn is the fact that the previous administration did not act on the facts and information contained in that report and they did not use the right judgment when they did act on the information. I think the hon. member is trying to twist that argument. I do not know if he intended to do that or not. He may have some justification for saying what he did on the basis of comments that were reported to have been made in some places but not by me in my territory.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think we need pay very much attention to the singularly unimpressive argument which has just been made because the Prime Minister himself answered that argument in the statement he made in this house, excerpts from which have already been read. He also answered it by going around the country calling this a hidden report-
It was.

If he gave it that name he was criticizing the government of that time because it did not produce it publicly; otherwise, why call it a hidden report? There is no point to the argument raised by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton and his argument has been met by the Prime Minister in the words that he used.
The report for 1958 has now been printed. Presumably it deals with the economic situation that obtains at the present time. Presumably it also deals with highly important matters such as employment and unemployment trends, the cost of living, gross national product estimates and questions of that nature. We are asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce to make this report public because of its importance and interest to this house and to the country. We have the right to do that because the Prime Minister himself attacked us so bitterly in accusing us of not making a similar report public a year ago. At that time he said-certainly by inference if not in words-that he would take a different course if he were in power. Well, he is now in power. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he is prepared to follow the

Supply-Trade and Commerce course advocated by the Prime Minister, that he does not disagree with the stand taken by the Prime Minister. All right, let him follow that course and either make the report public or else publicly repudiate the argument of the Prime Minister at this time.
Mr. Chairman, in replying to a question on this subject some time ago I believe the Prime Minister said that the report for 1958 would be made available in 1959.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Chairman, I think we must express some amazement at hearing the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton so neatly repudiate the Prime Minister. I want to recall to the committee that the Prime Minister's accusation against the former administration was that for political purposes it concealed the document. I want to bring out the dates. The date of the document is March 1957. They are prepared in March of each year. The date of the election, as the supporters of the government are so wont to remind us, was June 10, 1957. The former government went out of office on June 21,
1957.	The attack of the Prime Minister was that the Liberal administration prior to June 21, 1957, had not published that document in the same year as that of its publication.
Hidden, hidden.

If that is so, how can the Minister of Trade and Commerce claim to be consistent and do other than repudiate his Prime Minister if he now takes the position that on July 19, 1958, he is unwilling to table the corresponding report prepared in March of 1958? Surely his position is that he must either table the document in accordance with the policy announced by his Prime Minister or repudiate and change that policy. Of course, a change in the policy involves the repudiation of the stand taken by the Prime Minister.

Mr. Chairman, I read
Hansard for the date in question, January 20,
1958,	last evening and again today. I suggest that what was said on that occasion is open to no other reasonable interpretation than that it was in substance a charge that the previous government having full knowledge of certain facts failed to act upon them. The use of the words "hidden" or "concealed" was simply the use of these words as adjectives and the charge contained no suggestion that the report should have been made public.
You had better read it again.
I am just about to do that.

You are in a jam and
you know it.

On page 3527 of Hansard for January 20, 1958, there is the following:
What action did the government take with regard to any of these matters? Parliament was sitting. But they did nothing during the session to bring about changes in legislation to meet the situation of which they had been warned.
That was the pith and substance of the entire speech made at that time. To carry on, on page 3528-
Just before the hon. member leaves that page-
Sit down.
I am just about finished.
-would the hon. member permit a question?
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Peace River has the floor. Will he permit a question by the hon. member for Ottawa West?

I am just about finished and after that I will permit a question. On page 3528 carrying on from where the hon. member for Essex East left off, there is the following:
Why did they not act on them, even if they did not think fit to reveal them?
And again:
Why did they not act when the house was sitting in January, February, March and April?
This, Mr. Chairman, is the essence of the charges that were the subject of that speech.

Will the hon. member now permit my question? He quoted from page 3527 and I would ask him to tell me what meaning he gives to these words of the Prime Minister who was referring to the opposition: "And now, for political purposes, having concealed this document." The hon. member will remember that the Prime Minister was doing a great deal of waving of the document in his hand at the time. Would he explain to us what the Prime Minister meant by those words?

A number of accusations had been made against the previous government but the major one was the failure to act on this information. The other was subsidiary. I imagine that is probably the explanation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

No. We cannot let the impression stand which has been created by the hon. member who has just spoken and, if I may say so, spoken very well. He has proved to be an excellent advocate. I understand that he is a lawyer

and I am sure he has had considerable training in the advocacy of bad causes. The case for which he has now taken a brief is obviously in that category. But in the very words my hon. friend has quoted therein lies the judgment we are making against the administration-"which the government of the day did not see fit to reveal." Those words, in addition to the words quoted by the hon. member for Ottawa West a few moments ago, clearly indicate that the Prime Minister was seeking to impart to the Canadian people that the previous administration had failed to reveal certain facts notwithstanding, as he himself said, that they were in a report marked "secret" and "confidential" and which he characterized as a hidden report. If that is not enough, if the words which my hon. friend himself has quoted are not sufficient, let me remind him again of the words referred to by the hon. member of Ottawa West.
We were on the slide, really on the slide, when they left power on June 21, and now, for political purposes, having concealed this document, they have the effrontery to pretend to the Canadian people-
And so on. "Having concealed this document"-those words, applying the ordinary rules of interpretation, clearly mean, as the hon. gentleman who has just spoken knows, but one thing, that is, that the previous administration had deliberately withheld from the Canadian people certain information. That is the charge. That was the charge made by the Prime Minister on January 20 last and we are saying now that no method of advocacy by anyone sitting opposite can change the implication of the literal meaning of those words. We are now charging that those who laid this indictment against the former administration stand condemned by their own very words, and we are asking them now to live up to the indictment they made against us-
They were not sincere.

-and to establish clearly to the Canadian people that in the making of that charge they were sincere. If the government today, through the Minister of Trade and Commerce, refuses to accede to the request made on this side, then the judgment of the house can only be one thing, that the Prime Minister and his colleagues were not sincere when they made this charge on January 20 last.
Mr. Chairman, I think it is essential at this point to put the record straight.
You cannot.

On June 18, 1958 a motion appeared on the order paper for the production of a copy of "The Canadian Economic
Supply-Trade and Commerce Outlook for 1958" as prepared by the Department of Trade and Commerce. The motion was proposed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. The Prime Minister replied, as found at page 1391 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, the government finds it necessary to oppose this motion on the ground that "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958" is a confidential document.
He went on to say later:
-we will produce it immediately after this year ends. It is a current report, publication of which would be detrimental until January, 1959.
In the course of the discussion on that occasion the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, in accordance with the rule which permits same, asked that his motion be set down as a notice of motion for debate. In routine proceedings and orders of the day for Saturday, July 19 you will find listed on page 16 under "Notices of Motion" No. 46 which is in these words:
June 18-Mr. Pickersgill-That an order of the house to issue for a copy of "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958" as prepared by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Obviously the house is seized of a notice of motion providing for a debate on this subject. I submit, sir, that we are out of order now-
Closure.
-in discussing the production of "The Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958", to which in any case a sufficient answer was given by the Prime Minister on June 18 of this year.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, of course we are not out of order in discussing this report in connection with the appropriation for the economic branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce on these estimates. It is obvious that we can discuss this on the estimates irrespective of what may be on the order paper in some other capacity. There is no doubt about that. The minister's remarks have been extremely interesting. The action taken by the Prime Minister last year has accomplished its purpose. Let us forget about it. The minister has said that the Prime Minister has already replied to this point in connection with the economic report for 1958 by saying that it should not be produced until January, 1959. If this is the right stand to take with regard to the economic report for 1958, I ask the minister if he will not agree that the right stand for any government to have taken with regard to the economic report for 1957 would have been to produce it in January, 1958. If that is true, what justification of any kind is there for the attack of the Prime Minister on the previous

Supply-Trade and Commerce government because, as the Prime Minister said, they concealed it in the spring of 1957?

Mr. Chairman, I find it difficult to relate these statements and this suggestion for a decision on my part as to what was said a year ago to the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the present year.

Perhaps we can help the minister a little bit. If he means that he cannot relate the things that were said by the Prime Minister before the election to those said on June 18 after the election, then there will be many people in this country who will have sufficient regard for our system to regret that he takes that stand.
I cannot relate it to the estimates of this year.

We will relate it directly to the estimates of this year. What is before us now is a vote to provide, among other things, for the publishing of an economic report for the benefit of the government by this department. Last session, on January 20, the Prime Minister took a stand on the issue in very sharp terms, and in very picturesque speech. There are some other adjectives I could use-
One of the best speeches ever made in the house.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce describes it as the best speech the Prime Minister ever made in the house.
Oh, oh.

Hon. members opposite applaud that. It was a very theatrical speech. The Prime Minister had a document in his hand which he waved about a great deal during the course of his speech, and that document was the report about which we are now speaking, the report for the year 1957.
As a matter of fact it may be rather interesting to hon. members opposite, who may not know, that when the Prime Minister spoke about the document, at that time, it had a substantial part of the blue cover still on it. The cover was torn off before it was brought into the house. At what point it was torn off, I do not know. However, I noted at the time the part of the blue cover, which he seemed to know nothing about, was there while he was waving the document with such a theatrical wave.
Did the hon. gentleman say it was torn off by him?

No, I was very careful not to say that. I could not prove that. I leave it to the hon. member for Huron to draw his own conclusions. The Prime Minister is now coming in, so for his benefit I shall repeat


what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said. He said the Prime Minister had made the best speech he has ever made in the house. I was referring to this document, and I said he waved it about a good deal. I have described the piece of blue cover that was on it while he was waving it. He took the position, and was severely critical-
What are these straw men?

He says now, what are these straw men? I do not regard this as a straw man.
He accused the opposition, for political purposes, of having concealed this document, of having failed to publish it before June 21, 1957. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says this year's report cannot be tabled; that it is not proper to table it now. He is now changing the policy as announced by his Prime Minister in refusing to table it now. I respectfully suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it is of very real interest if the Prime Minister can take that stand, and then follow it up by making references across this country to what he called the hidden report. Then having received the acclaim of the voters of this country, and their support in a very large measure which I must admit, having taken that position, his Minister of Trade and Commerce now takes a directly opposite position about the publishing of this year's report. It is a matter of some significance that the voters of this country should be treated in that way by the government. It is not a straw man, as the Prime Minister would lead us to believe. I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce, therefore, if he does not agree that this is a change in policy on the part of the government a repudiation of the policy as announced by his Prime Minister on January 20, 1958.

I reiterate. I am not repudiating the stand taken by the Prime Minister. In fact, I set the record straight by reading out what the Prime Minister said on June 18 of this year. I subscribed to that stand with regard to the economic report for 1958.
Would the minister, then, just explain to us how he reconciles the difference between the stand taken on June 18, and the stand taken on January 20?
The circumstances are not the same.
Perhaps I could deal with the interjection.
I say the circumstances are not the same.
No election.
No, that is not the point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; the hon. member for Ottawa West has the floor.

The hon. member for Athabasca says that the circumstances are not the same, and that is quite right. The whole point is that the circumstances are not the same. The Prime Minister was speaking on January 20 before an election on March 31. The election was held, and then on June 18 he was in office and the election was over so he was repudiating the position taken on January 20.

Recently I have been wondering why the Prime Minister arrives in the house so often at the appropriate time. I have just discovered the reason. I had to send to the reading room for today's issue of the Journal because there were none in circulation, and I have just read an article by Richard Jackson entitled "Hill Talk". It says:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker has had his centre block office wired for sound.
House of Commons sound.
He's done what every parliamentarian has dreamed of doing since electronics were invented . . . arranged things so that he may work in his office and still keep up-to-the-last word track of what is going on in the commons.
I can scarcely credit that being done with consent of the house, Mr. Chairman, but I should like the Prime Minister to inform the house if this report is correct.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question asked by the hon. member for Kootenay West might be very interesting, but it is not relevant to the item under discussion.

Surely the hon. member has raised a very important question of privilege. He has quoted a newspaper article to the effect that, in some way, without the knowledge of the house or without consultation with or consent of the house or any of its officers, somebody has done something to wire the house to the Prime Minister's office so that the Prime Minister can follow what is going on here by an electronic method. This is the first I have heard about it, but it is a very important question of privilege which should be decided.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must bring to the attention of the Leader of the Opposition that the member for Kootenay West did not raise this matter as a question of privilege. I believe also that this question should be taken up when the Speaker is in the chair.

I shall turn it into a question of privilege, and ask the Prime Minister if this report is correct.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

Mr. Chairman, it is a rather serious matter if the equipment recording the proceedings in this house have been tapped without the consent of the house. I am in some doubt as to whether the chairman can deal with it, but it is a very serious matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind hon. members that at the moment the only item that can be discussed is vote 396, which deals with matters about which hon. members know.
A question of privilege can be raised at any time in the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, a question of privilege can be raised in the committee. But the hon. member for Kootenay West did not bring it forward as a question of privilege.
Mr. Chairman, when I found out I had not brought it forward in the proper manner I changed it to a question of privilege and I think that stands.
If it is a question of privilege, it is a rather serious thing and I would hope that the Prime Minister would see fit to deal with it because-
Mr. Chairman-
I have the floor.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The rights of parliament!
Hitler.
The hon. member who is speaking-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: We have not got dictatorship yet.
You have no question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I will ask hon.
members kindly to permit the hon. member who has the floor to carry on with his remarks. It is quite difficult to understand what the hon. member has to say with people all yelling at once. At the present time the hon. member for Ottawa West has the floor.
Mr. Chairman, if I could have the floor-
No.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member for Ottawa West has the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. member for Ottawa West relinquish the floor to the Prime Minister?
As soon as I have finished my remarks I will do so.

That indicates how serious the matter is.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Mr. Chairman, I was going to say that if this report is true, it is a serious matter affecting this house and the proceedings of this house.
You have said that three times now. Don't be so repetitious.

It means that it is possible, once the wire is taken outside in that way, to have it wired or sent by long distance phone anywhere in the world, and to have anyone brought in for the purpose of listening. Where does the thing stop? Are our caucus rooms wired? Are our private telephones tapped or where does the matter stop?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must once again remind hon. members-
Possibly I could speak to this matter now, Mr. Chairman. I realize that hon. gentlemen opposite have very little to talk about.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: That is why you are always out of the house.
You do your best thinking when you are in the seated position, I would say to the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You are very kind.

Much has been made of this matter. The hon. gentleman who raised it did so very properly, may I say immediately, knowing the country whence he came and his regard for parliamentary institutions there. This is the course followed in the United Kingdom in order to permit the prime minister to have available to him, so that there will not be any loss of time through missing a portion of debate, what is happening in the house. This installation was made with the authority of the department in order to make available to myself in the last few days, in view of the serious nature of what is taking place, an opportunity that would otherwise be denied me because I cannot be in the house all the time. There is available, in my office-and there is no concealment whatever-whenever the debate is on a private loudspeaker which enables me to follow the debate to the end that I can be back at any moment that I am required. That is the practice that is followed in the United Kingdom-I do not know whether or not it has been followed by successive prime ministers but it is the practice there-in order to enable the prime minister to discharge two of his responsibilities, namely to carry out his responsibility to be in the house when required and at the same time to maintain the very serious duties that fall on him. In spite of all the agitated-I

almost said synthetic-exaggeration on the part of those opposite, there is nothing whatsoever in the nature of disregard of parliament. It is a desire fully to regard parliament.
Some prime ministers have stayed in the house at all times and others have not done so. As I remember Mr. King, he used to leave the house quite regularly because of the impossibility of being here on all occasions. Realizing that I did not want to miss what was going on but wanted to have a realization of the debates, to the end that the contribution being made is always available to me, I have that device available in my office. In order that there may be no misunderstanding, I may say that it was installed just a couple of days ago in order to permit and enable me to carry on the two responsibilities, one the very heavy one at this time of being required to meet an international situation that those who have had the responsibility know of and at the same time not to disregard my duty to the House of Commons.

Now that we are on this point, Mr. Chairman, may I say that it is quite obvious that something has happened- whatever the reasons may be for it-that is unprecedented in parliamentary history, something that has never happened before and something which I think is extremely important. Whatever the reasons may be for it, the result is that the proceedings of this house, as they are taking place, can now be heard outside of this house. That is a new development in our parliamentary traditions and in our parliamentary history; and I suggest that what has happened in the United Kingdom or in any other place has no particular bearing on the matter. I know, of course, that the Prime Minister has great responsibilities and that he cannot be in this house all the time. I know that this is a particularly difficult time for him. But I also know that his predecessor, Mr. St. Laurent, had great responsibilities. He was the head of a government in times of crisis and at that time there was no suggestion that in order to make the work a little bit easier and so that he could cover both the house and his office this should be done. I am also perfectly certain that if Mr. St. Laurent had wished it to be done, he would have taken this matter up in the House of Commons and informed the House of Commons of what was happening and perhaps have secured permission of the House of Commons so members would not be put in a position where they would read about such a change in the columns of a local newspaper. I suggest also, Mr. Chairman, that that is the way we should have been treated in this matter.

I remember very well indeed-and the Prime Minister must remember it also-that in one of the committees of this house a few years ago-it happened to be the committee on external affairs-in order to facilitate our work and in order to make it a little bit easier for the reporters and for the record of the committee to be circulated quickly, for one experimental meeting of the committee we introduced some electronic device into that room which would record what was said for reproduction and circulation. I remember that the leader of the Conservative party at that time rose in his place in this house and attacked the government of the day very vigorously indeed because of this breach of parliamentary privilege. As a result of the stand that he took at that time we ceased to use this electronic device.
If the Prime Minister feels that the time has come that he needs this kind of assistance in order to keep in touch with the house- and I am not expressing myself on that matter one way or the other at the present time-I think it would have been consistent with the privileges of this house for the Prime Minister who brought the matter up to have consulted the house and obtained permission of the house for himself and perhaps for some others who might also benefit by this kind of device.
