397. International Trade Relations Branch, including a fee of $6,000 to the International Customs Tariffs Bureau, $204,248.

World trade relations have taken on a very significant aspect since the Soviet union launched its economic offensive against the west some three years ago. Russian determination to capture and hold world markets, by whatever means necessary, is nothing short of a formidable offensive against the west and its success thus far, as surely as I stand here, is one of the main underlying causes for the recession through which we are passing and from which we will have difficulty in emerging unless we do more than we are doing now.
While in Paris last fall I took the time to visit, for instance, two of the largest buyers of pulpwood in France to see if they could not resume the purchases of pulpwood from Canada which they had been making for many, many years. In each case I interviewed the president of the company and in each case I was accompanied by Mr. Robert Campbell Smith, our commercial attache in Paris. In each case the pattern was the same -these companies had in the past bought their pulpwood from Canada but had lately shifted their source of supply to Russia. Why? In each case the reason was because they got
Supply-Trade and Commerce a better deal from Russia. Both presidents mentioned that the quality of the Russian wood was good, the contracts with Russia were carried out to the letter and no complaints arose about the quality or quantity involved, even though the French company did not send scalers to Russia to inspect the wood before shipment. Moreover, shipping dates were met on time, on the dates agreed upon, but in spite of all these things both company presidents expressed the desire to buy from Canada. For one thing Canadian pulpwood is less expensive but the haul being longer costs a little more; I understand our shippers get something like $39 a cord for pulpwood on the dock in Canada, while the cost in Russia runs around $48 a cord on the dock. Shipping costs tend to equalize the landed costs but Russian pulpwood landed in France costs a little more than Canadian pulpwood.
Hon. members might ask why these companies insist on buying from Russia if it is cheaper for them to buy Canadian pulpwood? The answer is simple; they get a better deal from that country than they can get from Canada. Russia will accept their currency while we sit back and insist on dollars. Russia does business how and where it can be done and as long as we do not realize that these countries simply cannot buy from us in the currency we insist upon, as long as we stick to our policies of "Take it on our terms or leave it", let me assure the house it is being left.
Furthermore, Russia has more aggressive and more expert selling agents and the impression they give to buying countries is this; "We want the business and we will do what we have to do to get it." In particular with reference to Canadian aluminum they say flatly, "We will undersell Canada regardless of how low Canadian prices are or may become." In other words, they are better horse traders, bargainers, they are better dealers and they get the business while we are losing our markets.
From Paris I went to London and with the help of our high commissioner, Mr. George Drew, I saw and talked to several of the main buyers of lumber from Canada, men like Sir Edward Monkhouse, who know our industries and who know Canada almost as well as we know it and have been buying our lumber for generations, men who are attached to Canada and have feelings of regard for the Canadian people. The story here is the same, Russia is supplying their lumber. Russia has captured our long-established lumber market and the Soviet union will do anything it has to do to get and keep the business.
They will, for instance, take pounds sterling in payment and will accept the buyer's note

Supply-Trade and Commerce for several months, in some cases without interest. As I say they will tell you point-blank, "We have come here to get the lumber market and we will do whatever we have to do to get it." This is what the lumber buyers in England tell us-with the Soviet union it is just as simple as that.
What is the reaction of the English lumber buyer? It is simply that he is forced to buy from Russia rather than from Canada, despite his feeling for a commonwealth nation. Our trade policies place him in the position where he cannot turn down the advantages of dealing with the Soviet union as opposed to Canada. Therefore, in an area such as my own, where our people depend on the sale of lumber and pulpwood for a living, things are rough. One of the provincial ministers of labour said the other day that the conditions in my riding were worse than any other riding in this country and that is, I have no doubt, correct. Already we see in visible and touching form the results of the loss of our markets to Russia and to a certain extent to Sweden and Finland. I am speaking of pulpwood and lumber which, after all, is what we have to sell in order to survive.
Of course Russia's trade offensive is not the only reason for the unprecedented extent of unemployment and suffering in my riding, but it is one of the main causes. Tight money in particular and our monetary policies in general, in addition to our trade policies, have all played an active part-
And your administration.

-in bringing about this situation.
In visiting my riding recently I found a family where the children had to leave for school without breakfast in the morning and another family which had six potatoes left without a cent with which to buy anything else. These conditions are general in several villages and naturally these people are very concerned. Some of them almost caused an insurrection at St. Quentin the other day because they had nothing to eat and nothing to do. Some of these people blame the government and some of their criticism is not warranted-like that of the man in my riding who said the other day, "Fishing is poor, the weather is bad, times are hard and you Conservatives are in."
Hear, hear.

But much of the criticism is warranted but it behooves this government to sit up and take notice. In many fields the government has shown bold initiative and has done what could be done to create employment; for instance, in the field of public works this government has done more for my riding

in seven months than all other governments put together have done since confederation.
Hear, hear.

This is the only government in the history of Canada which has listened to us and has recognized and acted upon our problems, but this government in some other fields, unfortunately, has not implemented its policies fast enough to permit effective results and has not taken the even drastic means necessary to create conditions conducive to full employment, thus removing suffering and hardship which weigh heavily upon our people.
I have dealt on many other occasions with other factors involved but, speaking now only in regard to trade, I would like to suggest, request and may even demand a more aggressive and effective trade policy with respect to foreign trade. Let us face it, we are living in times when the Soviet trade offensive is not only taking away our markets, and is eminently successful in doing so, but their planned trade offensive will intensify as time goes on.
We must take steps to compete and compete successfully and to do this, in my mind, there are three fundamental requirements with respect to changes in the attitude on the part of federal governments, and this applies to all governments. In the first instance we must sell. I have always felt and I still feel that what Canada most needs is a battalion of live-wire agents, of good bargainers-horse traders if you want to call them that-going from country to country and buyer to buyer, selling Canada and Canada's products. Such agents should have specific instructions on how and what to promote and sell. Many countries simply do not know what we have to sell. We missed the boat at the world fair.
Secondly, we must take measures which will permit us to sell, which will require a complete re-evaluation of our monetary policies, among other things, to enable us to accept soft currencies or any currency of value. It is nothing short of national snobbishness to refuse to accept the pound sterling. In other words, we must adopt the means to sell. President Eisenhower underlined our problem in this house the other day when he went out of his way to emphasize the battle between the west and the Soviet union for world trade, and which might well be the most important problem facing the west today. I believe it is, and I also believe we are not doing enough in Canada to play our part in that struggle.
Whether Russia wins by beating us with arms or starves us out by cornering and capturing our markets, the consequences will be the same. We must adopt the attitude that we will succeed, and be prepared to

take all honest means at our command. Thus, barter and all that this term involves; currency, in whatever usable form it comes; credit, in whatever acceptable form it is offered, must become part of our trade policies. Time is running against us. We have lost the momentum. We are dragging our feet.
Coming to the third point, may I say that however great the need for agents is, and important as the need for changes in our monetary system is, let us not forget that the product speaks for itself. One of the complaints I heard often in England is that Russian lumber is better cut than Canadian lumber. We here depend on portable mills where it is next to impossible to maintain exact dimensions, while in Russia the mills are fixed, and fastened down and equipped in a way which allows for practically no variations in dimensions. In England, people build their houses with rough lumber, and unless the widths are rigidly maintained it is hard to put floor covering, for example, over the lumber.
The need for a better Canadian product- and this applies to all manufactured goods- is of primary importance if we are to recapture our markets and create new ones. This is one reason why I very much appreciate the steps being taken by the government to set up an organization to help small industry. Of course, this proposed organization, at least as I understand it now, does not go far enough. I hope the scope will be enlarged to include capital assistance, product perfection and selling techniques. We have a selling job to do. We have not been doing it in the past. Let us buckle down and begin doing it now.
Would the minister tell the house what steps are being taken to improve trade relations within the different countries of the western hemisphere?

Mr. Chairman, this branch is engaged in that activity at all times. Through our trade commissioners, and through talks between officials of this department and representatives of foreign governments we keep constantly in touch with the situation with respect to trade relations between Canada and other countries of the western hemisphere.

The member for Resti-gouche-Madawaska has just brought up a question which is very important in northern New Brunswick. I asked the minister two questions on this same matter last evening. Can he tell us, now that he has his officials with him, what the Department of Trade and Commerce is doing to bring back to normal our exports of pulpwood to the European
Supply-Trade and Commerce market? The hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska has cited figures and said he is aware from his personal contacts with dealers in France and Britain that our prices are no higher than the prices paid for Russian pulp. In fact, they are even lower.

One thing that must be borne in mind is that the demand for pulp-wood all over the world is down at the present moment. The government, in so far as it has trade commissioners stationed abroad, keeps in touch with the process of trade, but the government is not involved actively and directly in selling pulpwood or any other article with the exception of wheat where we have a crown corporation to deal with its disposal. Private industry has representatives abroad who push these sales of pulpwood as is done with regard to other products.

I really believe this is a question which should be dealt with. The minister says the government does not try to sell, that it is not a salesman to sell goods manufactured in Canada. We should have an organization of salesmen around the world able to sell the products which we manufacture here. We manufacture much more than we can consume, and unless these goods are sold on the markets of the world we are due to have a recession which will last not only for a year or two but for a long time. I believe the Department of Trade and Commerce should organize salesmen around the world to sell these products.

We are not engaged in state trading. We have our trade commissioner service in these 45 countries round the world whose business it is-and they are very active in this-to call upon businessmen in the countries in which they are located, to communicate with Canadian businessmen who visit those countries or to write to them. Information is constantly furnished to these officials who in turn pass it on to the government and to Canadian businessmen here. A great deal has been published in that magnificent booklet of ours called "Foreign Trade". So every possible step is taken by the officials of this department to keep Canadian business informed of opportunities abroad. But we have not yet reached the stage where we employ salesmen under government auspices to sell goods produced in Canada by private industry.
Canadian businessmen are themselves very active. As I mentioned on Thursday, 4,000 visits to the various countries of the world abroad have been paid by Canadian businessmen, and that is the way in which our Canadian trade is advanced. It is by the means I mentioned that business is kept informed of what is going on.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I have listened to what the minister has had to say, but I listened earlier to what was said by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska. He said a while ago that while he was in France and in England he learned that we were losing the pulp-wood trade to Russia. On account of what? If we have commissioners over there looking after trade, and if they have not reported, as they should have reported, that for some reason or another we are losing this trade, there is something wrong somewhere and this should be corrected by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
We are facing the same situation with regard to newsprint. We are losing our world trade to Norway, Sweden and Finland. How is it that we are losing our trade with the United States with respect to a product which otherwise has to be imported from so far away? We want to know what is wrong, in order that we may be able to change this situation, and that is why we are asking the minister to make the changes necessary for us to be able to sell our products.

As I have said, in some respects trade has fallen off. Nevertheless, Canada is the greatest supplier of lumber and pulpwood, and our agents abroad are very active in promoting those sales by getting the information that is required. It is a matter of economics. If the Russians offer products below the price of Canadian products they sometimes get the business. I spoke about this the other day when we were dealing with aluminum.
Here is an example of a sale of lumber and lumber products amounting to $889,000 which came about through the activities of one of our trade commissioners in the United States. He made an extensive survey of lumber outlets in Michigan and Ohio during 1956 which, extended in 1957, formed the basis of many inquiries which resulted in a substantial volume of new business. Canadian lumber lists and special offerings were made available to local firms while, conversely, the names and interests of local firms were circulated to the industry in Canada. Items of new business to the amount I have mentioned-$889,000-were reported in 1957 as being due to this phase of the trade commissioner's activity.
I have here a list covering at least a dozen pages indicating various items of all types where the activity of trade commissioners resulted in business for Canadian firms. Here is another item coming from Mexico City. The commercial counsellor there, our trade commissioner, brought a Mexico City firm in touch with a Canadian company as a result of which seven orders for newsprint to the value of $65,000 were placed. Here is another

from New Orleans. The names of various British Columbia and Ontario suppliers were furnished to firms in South Carolina, Oklahoma, California, Texas, Alabama and Florida by the trade commissioner as a result of which sales of lumber and other products were made to the extent of $813,000. And so it goes all the way through this book covering anything from diesel locomotives to codfish, aluminum, brewer's malt and durum wheat and so on. It is a very active branch of the government.

Mr. Chairman, may I direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Instead of sending 50 people on a trade mission to Great Britain, all expenses paid, would it not be just as reasonable to spend some money in sending representatives from various manufacturing and industrial concerns as well as representatives of the minister's department to various countries of the world to stimulate Canadian trade abroad? What is the point of sending 50 men to Great Britain to say, "Please, manufacturers of the United Kingdom, sell us some goods". Most of these things are already produced in this country. I think it would be advisable to spend $100,000 or more in sending someone from the minister's department together with representatives of those industries whose goods are in a surplus position in Canada to make some sales abroad and elsewhere. I do not think it is useful to send 50 men on a mission at the same time so they can have a nice pleasure trip. It is not necessary for them to have such a happy time and they could have accomplished more than merely saying to the British manufacturers, "Please, for God's sake, sell us some goods. We are not able to manufacture our own goods or buy and sell them". I believe the suggestion I have advanced is far more reasonable.

Mr. Chairman, a while ago the minister said we have an organization which seeks to sell Canadian goods in foreign markets. Despite this fact we have lost a great deal of our trade in pulpwood as the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska proved with the figures he had on the subject. He was on the spot and he asked a question.
In addition to the loss of pulpwood sales we have lost some sales of aluminum to Russia. I believe something is wrong somewhere. If it is not with our economy then it must be with our system of distribution. There should be an organization in the department to study what is wrong with us so we can recuperate the trade we lost. That is what I am asking the minister at this

time. Is there any organization in the Department of Trade and Commerce to try to ascertain what is wrong with our system so we can recuperate our losses?

Mr. Chairman, I will repeat what I have said. The trade commissioner's branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce is one of the most efficient branches of the government. Hon. members on all sides of the house have paid tribute to the work that is being done by these men of ours abroad. They are all carefully selected and trained. After serving abroad for a period they return to Canada and make contacts with Canadian industry and then take up their posts abroad. Every week letters come to me or to the department from businessmen who have been abroad and in contact with our trade commissioners and they report that they have received excellent cooperation and benefited greatly by the advice and counsel given by the trade commissioners.
Had it not been for the work of these men abroad Canada's export trade would not be higher at this time than it was a year ago and, as I pointed out yesterday, it has been rising.

Mr. Chairman, I admit that we have a very good staff in the department and I wish to join with those hon. members who have spoken in praise of the work that has been done by this personnel. However, aside from that, we are losing some trade. We should not be losing trade because we certainly cannot furnish France or England with the pulp they need through lack of orders. There must be a reason for this. If a special study were made concerning pulp-wood, newsprint and aluminum it might be possible to discover this reason. We are losing trade at the present time and we should be in a position to know why we are losing it so we can correct the difficulty. If we do not study the matter we will not know where we stand. Canada continues to suffer from over-production which creates a condition of recession and everybody wants to get rid of that.

Mr. Chairman, the hon member's suggestion will be given very careful study by the officials of the department and myself. I gave an example the other day of the difficulties we face and the commodity I chose for the purpose of illustration was aluminum. We are the world's great supplier of aluminum and yet Russian competition has interfered with our sales of aluminum abroad. The hon. member said we should do something about it. We have done all that we could do about it but if the Russians are prepared, as they have stated, to quote a price that is under our price regardless of
Supply-Trade and Commerce at what level we set it, then we are really in difficulty.
We have communicated with the United Kingdom asking them to continue to purchase Canadian aluminum and resist the sale of aluminum from Russia. That is the type of action we take. The various branches of this department are constantly in touch with trends of business all across the world. Reports come in all the time with regard to what is happening in respect of one commodity or another. The businessmen of this country secure that information from our department. We maintain close touch with world economic conditions.

399. Canadian participation in the Brussels universal and international exhibition 1958, $709,628.

Mr. Chairman, the minister will probably recall that I asked him some questions a few weeks ago about the situation with respect to the Brussels universal and international exhibition. I do not know whether or not he has had occasion to personally visit the exhibition but he will recall there were some articles published in the newspapers in criticism of it, and there was also some criticism made by one member of his own party who was there some weeks ago. Under the circumstances and due to the fact that this exhibition is costing the country $3 million I believe we are entitled to expect some comment from the minister concerning the exhibition. I should also like to have him give us a little more information about the circumstances surrounding the resignation of Mrs. Bienvenue. We have little information at the present time to use as the basis of a discussion of this subject. We have received only the information the minister gave us and have had tabled the letter of resignation and the minister's reply. I would appreciate very much if the minister would be kind enough to give us more information so we will have a clearer picture of the situation at the Brussels universal and international exhibition.

Mr. Chairman, the plans for the Canadian exhibit at the Brussels universal and international exhibition were made by the former Liberal administration several years ago and the money was allocated very largely during the lifetime of that administration.
When we came into the picture at the end of June, 1957, the plans were very far advanced and most of the money had then been voted for this purpose. We were presented with a fait accompli in the type of
2454	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce building which had been designed, the exhibits that were going to be shown in the building, the beautification of the grounds surrounding the building and the selection of the site on which the building would rest. Virtually all the appointments with regard to the management of the exhibition had been made, including the appointment of Madame Bienvenue as chaperone. That was done by order in council in that period of interregnum between June 10 and June 21.
Some people have been very critical of the Canadian exhibit at Brussels and a much larger number have been very complimentary of it. For a long time I kept a record from week to week of the letters coming in and the comments made. For quite a while they were about 50-50, 50 per cent condemning the Canadian exhibit and 50 per cent praising it. Latterly I have received no letters finding fault with the Canadian exhibit but an increasing number of comments praising it. Some of these comments are now coming from visitors to the exhibition living overseas in Belgium, Holland, France and elsewhere in Europe. They are very much impressed with the Canadian exhibit. Thousands of them have been through our pavilion and the number is steadily increasing.
It is important to recall what was the purpose of the world exhibition. The original invitation which came from the authorities at Brussels to the Canadian government was expressed in the following words:
We want it to be possible for any one nation to be able to explain to all other nations how it lives, what are its religious and philosophic conceptions, its economic and social achievements. If to govern means an attempt to give a people happiness then let the nations tell each other just how they visualize that happiness and how they would assure the required material and moral conditions.
It will be seen from that that this is not a trade fair or an industrial exhibition, and people have become confused in their minds with regard to that. It is intended to depict the Canadian way of life and I think that is being done by our exhibit in Brussels. There is an industrial section. Art is shown and various other aspects of life in Canada are depicted.
One must also remember that although the amount of money, $3 million, seems sufficiently large for such an enterprise it is dwarfed by the amount of money spent by the United States, Russia and some other countries who have very large exhibits adjacent to the Canadian pavilion. But, as I have stated on another occasion, Canada in spending $3 million on this exhibit has played a part comparable to that of other nations of similar size. We have not seen fit to enlarge


the amount of money available for the Canadian exhibit. We took it for granted that the former administration had given very careful consideration to the planning and that within the financial limit set satisfactory results could be achieved. I think that satisfactory results have been achieved.
There were complaints earlier about the food in the restaurant. You hear complaints about the food in the restaurant upstairs here and I have been around these parts now for over eight years. The cost of the meals in the Canadian restaurant at Brussels was under question and the cost was subsequently lowered. Canadian restaurant people were given an opportunity to tender on providing meals over there but did not take up the offer. A Belgian restaurant keeper undertook to provide meals. He had the impression that visitors to the exhibition from Canada and North America generally would like to have food that is common to Europe. Some of our Canadian visitors apparently did not want that. They wanted, I suppose, ham and egs, hamburgs, hot dogs and things of that nature.
I hope codfish.

Others who are interested in seeing how other people live have not objected to the type of meals served in the restaurant. Complaints about the restaurant, although they were fairly numerous in the early stages, have declined. I have not heard any complaint about the restaurant recently. In any case, a visitor to the Brussels exhibition is not compelled to eat in the Canadian restaurant. Every other exhibit there has its restaurant and there are other public eating places in Brussels. I think we do not need to magnify too much complaints of individuals with regard to this or that. You cannot satisfy people with regard to art, architecture, food and a long list of other things where opinions differ depending upon people's tastes, background, training and so on.
A staff of 48 students has been over there since early in April acting as guides, 24 young women and 24 young men selected carefully from the universities of this country by university authorities on the basis of their academic standing and on the basis of their knowledge of languages. These carefully selected students were given the privilege of spending six months in Europe, earning a salary during that period, getting free lodging and free board and accumulating leave so that they would be able to do a little travelling in Europe. They are the most fortunate university students in Canada. There are hundreds of university students who would gladly have made the trip and acted as guides at the Brussels exhibition. It is the type of

opportunity that comes about once in a lifetime and by and large I think our students have been excellent representatives of Canada and have done a first-class piece of work over there.
A little trouble arose over the retirement of the chaperone but it was at her own request and I accepted her resignation. I took it for granted that if a person went to the trouble of carefully writing out a resignation and presenting it to me I had no alternative but to accept, and I accepted it as I would under any other circumstances. Resignations are not lightly written and I simply assumed that the matter had been very carefully considered. There was a little disturbance among some of the students at the time who thought that the chaperone's resignation should not have been accepted and there was some disturbance over whether or not her place would be taken by someone else. Her place was, of course, immediately taken over by another lady who has served as chaperone in the interval.
As of this week Madame Boisvert of Quebec city has been appointed to be chaperone at the Canadian exhibit at Brussels and will be leaving in a very few days to take up her new position. While she is en route and for a while after she arrives Miss Armstrong will continue to act in the capacity of chaperone.
Is that the wife of the sergeant of the R.C.M.P.?

No. Miss Armstrong is from our London office.
Miss Armstrong will stay there until Madame Boisvert becomes thoroughly familiar with the situation and with her duties.
This constitutes a report, Mr. Chairman, on the exhibition at Brussels. From what I can gather from reports from newspapers published on the continent, from letters written by newspapermen who have been over there and businessmen who have visited the place, it appears that the Canadian exhibit is a credit to Canada; that it is depicting Canadian life in acceptable fashion; that it compares very favourably with the exhibits of other nations. I think we can be proud of the Canadian exhibit. I think we can give a word of praise to those who conceived, planned it and put it into operation; a word of praise to the students and others who are assisting in giving a good Canadian welcome to the visitors to the Brussels world fair.

I should like, first of all, to thank the minister for the information he has just given to us. However, coming back to the case of Madame Bienvenue, I could
Supply-Trade and Commerce read from her letter to the minister in which she said:
I am having imposed on me obligations which go far beyond the terms of my contract.
May I ask the minister if he tried to ascertain whether or not what she alleges is true? Have new obligations been imposed upon Mrs. Bienvenue beyond the terms of her contract or agreement with the department?

Not to my knowledge. I had a report given to me with regard to this, and there was a thorough understanding concerning the terms of employment, salary and things of that nature. In the course of operation some misunderstanding must have arisen as to what should be done, and that is understandable in the operation of a world's fair. Madame Bienvenue considered she was being asked to do things that she had not expected to do, and was not being reimbursed to the extent she thought she should be. She indicated that she required an additional salary of $200 a month, and she said, and I quote her exact words:
Failing this, I resign my appointment 30 days from this date.

I understand that, according to the agreement, Madame Bienvenue was supposed to be the social counsellor and chaperone of the women students. According to information I have received, as well as newspaper reports, she was also called upon to act as concierge, housekeeper and sometimes charwoman. Surely if she was called upon to do more she was right in asking for more pay.
I do not believe for one minute that she was called upon to do the other duties to which my hon. friend has referred.

I do not know if you would call it a hotel where the students lived in Brussels, but I understand this was a four-storey house. There was no caretaker and there was no nurse. According to the information I have received, some of the students were sick and she had to take care of them. If she acted as nurse, charwoman and housekeeper, how could the minister blame her for asking for more money?
As a matter of fact, the letter she sent to the minister was not a letter of resignation. She mentioned to the minister she would resign if the conditions were not changed and if her salary was not increased because she was doing more work. I think she was quite right in asking for more pay. It is only logical to ask for more pay if her duties and obligations had been increased.

I have the greatest respect for Madame Bienvenue, Mr. Chairman. I think she performed her duties in admirable

Supply-Trade and Commerce fashion. I took her resignation at face value. I saw no reason why I should not accept it because we had no funds voted for this particular purpose. Had she indicated in her letter she wished to confer with regard to duties or confer with me regarding salary matters, that would have been different. But it was a letter of resignation, and I assumed that it had been carefully considered before it was written and signed.

Before the minister accepted the resignation of Madame Bienvenue did he try to ascertain from sources other than the reports he received from officials in Brussels what the exact situation was? I think we have a right to assume that something is not going too well out there because even the members of parliament have made complaints, not members of the opposition but members of the government. I believe the minister would have been justified in asking for a complete investigation in the situation. After all, when the Canadian people are spending $3 million they are entitled to get some benefit from it.

The complaints my hon. friend mentions made by members of parliament to my knowledge were complaints with regard to the nature of the exhibit, the size of the building, the type of food that was being served in the restaurant. I did not hear from any member of parliament about the duties of the chaperone. I heard commendatory remarks concerning Madame Bienvenue. Prior to her departure, I was assured she was the type of person who would fill this job admirably, and I believe she did. I did not feel justified in making any extra expenditures to conduct an investigation under the circumstances. If people are not happy in the work that they are doing, it is their privilege to offer their resignation. In this case, that was done and I accepted it.

I quite understand the minister's difficulty about assessing public opinion on the character and value of our exhibit in Brussels. It is quite impossible, of course, to participate in an exhibition of this kind and satisfy everybody. I, myself, am in no position to judge about the success of Canadian participation in this exhibit. Reports I have had would lead me to believe the effort was creditable, in view of the amount of money available, and that the exhibits are a reasonably attractive reflection of life in this country.
I should like to ask the minister one or two questions. Has there been any change in the plans for participation in the exhibit? I am thinking of the appearance, for instance, of the National Ballet or the Theatre du


Nouveau Monde. Has it been found necessary to cut down on some aspects of our participation and, if so, why was that required? The minister has touched upon the question of morale amongst the staff, and stated in the house that morale amongst the students was very high. Some of us have had letters from students which indicated that morale, in respect of some of them, was not too high.
However, there is something else that has been stated and I think this is a matter of some seriousness, namely that reports have been sent back by R.C.M.P. officers who are there on the conduct of the members of the staff. I should like to know from the minister whether, in fact, that has happened; whether the R.C.M.P. have taken it upon themselves to report to the government on the members of the Canadian staff at the exhibition.

I have no knowledge of any report by the R.C.M.P. with regard to the people engaged in activities at the Canadian pavilion. In any case, that matter does not come under my jurisdiction. The Minister of Justice would have to deal with that particular matter. On the earlier question of the Leader of the Opposition may I say this. I do not think there has been any reduction whatsoever in any of the programs planned for the Canadian exhibition at the Brussels fair.

The minister has just said that any reports that might be made by the R.C.M.P. would not be made to him and therefore he would perhaps not be aware of them. But the Canadian participation in the exhibition is, of course, under his jurisdiction. This matter has already been taken up in the house. On June 26 a question was addressed to the Minister of Justice on this point. He said that he would make inquiries to ascertain whether or not reports have been received. We have received information that such reports have been made. I think it would be well to clear this matter up. We had hoped that the Minister of Justice might have informed the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether, in fact, there is any basis to this kind of talk. We asked a question in the house. He said that he would make inquiries about it on June 26 but we have not heard anything since then.

As far as the Department of Trade and Commerce is concerned I can say that we have asked for no reports from the R.C.M.P.; we have received no reports from the R.C.M.P.; and we know of no reports sent back from the R.C.M.P. except, I am informed, that they complained about the food that they were receiving.

I think this question of the difficulty that is now taking place at the Brussels fair is most regrettable. I think it is most regrettable from the point of view of the students who had looked forward to this experience with a good deal of anticipation. I think it is unfortunate for them that there should have been this misunderstanding, as I would call it, as to the relationship between the members of the personnel at the Brussels fair. I know Mrs. Bienvenue and I also know that she is a person who would take on these responsibilities with a great deal of compunction and certainly would not take these duties lightly. I think she may not have entered in her letters all the reasons that may have provoked her resignation. I feel that there is a great deal more left unsaid than is said in the letter. Under these circumstances it would seem to me that the minister might well have utilized, for instance, our representatives in Belgium who were on the spot to make a very thorough inquiry as to the reasons why Mrs. Bienvenue tendered her resignation. I think there is a great deal more being left unsaid than is being said. I rather feel that it would not be asking too much of the department to ask it to make a thorough investigation as to exactly what is going on in the Brussels fair among our Canadian personnel. I wonder whether the minister would not perhaps tell us exactly who has been chosen to replace Mrs. Bienvenue. I understood him to say that it was a Mrs. Boisvert who was to replace Mrs. Bienvenue. But as the hon. member knows, there are a great number of families bearing the name of Boisvert. I wonder whether he could be more specific.

In reply to the earlier part of the hon. member's remarks may I say that I know of no dissatisfaction now prevailing among the staff at the Canadian pavilion at Brussels. As I said earlier, there was some dissatisfaction at the time of the resignation of Mrs. Bienvenue. As to her successor, in order to identify her a little bit more carefully may I say that she is Mrs. Claire Paquette Boisvert of Quebec city.

One of the things that impressed me greatly was the choice of the building, having regard to where the building was located. It was a very unfortunate choice that was made in taking that particular building. It was a building without very many services. One of the things that stands out is the fact that the R.C.M.P. and the staff were made to inhabit the same building. According to the information received from the R.C.M.P. this is against their regulations which demand that they be housed separately from the staff. Mrs. Bienvenue took the

Supply-Trade and Commerce trouble to call me into her office when I visited that building. Of course, she was very specific in her complaints. There is no question about it that the former government got this thing off to a bad start. I presume this government is doing everything it can to straighten the matter out. In the light of the more favourable opinions that are now being received, I also presume that this government has done quite a bit to ameliorate conditions at the fair. From speaking with people visiting our exhibition, talking with the guides and, what I personally could find out from simply going through it, looking around and asking questions, the fair is not a success. Canada is not doing a proper job as far as our participation in that fair is concerned. It is unfortunate that I am obliged to say that but, as far as I am concerned, that is what I have found.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I pursue the matter thai was originated by my friend the hon. member for Levis. A moment ago the minister said, if I understood him rightly, that he had received no reports from the R.C.M.P. Paragraph 4 of it reads as follows:
4. I have learned that three reports concerning the personnel of the Canadian residence (the Royal Canadian Mounted Police excepted) have been sent to Ottawa without my knowledge. The first is said to incorporate a grave rumour which libels the reputations of the 24 young women. The second, based on a minor incident, suggests that our young people use alcohol excessively. The third concerns me.
In the light of that statement, which seems to be in contradiction to what the minister has said, I wonder whether he will not comment on the situation anew?
I understand that these are charges made by Mrs. Bienvenue herself. You are reading from her letter?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was reading from the sessional paper which I take it is a letter from Mrs. Bienvenue to the minister.

Just in case a stranger might not know what a sessional paper is, let it be clear that this sessional paper is the original letter from Mrs. Bienvenue and addressed to me. It is not a government publication. These are the statements that were made. But I have already given my answer with regard to communications from the R.C.M.P.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Has the minister ever asked the Minister of Justice if there were reports such as those that are mentioned in that paragraph 4 of the letter?

Supply-Trade and Commerce
No, I have not made that inquiry of him.

Does not the minister think he should do that? This is a fairly serious charge made by the signer of this letter to the effect that reports of this kind have been sent back by the R.C.M.P. to Ottawa. I will draw to the attention of the Minister of Justice the interest of the hon. gentleman in this matter.

Does the minister mean he has not received any reports, not one of the reports mentioned in the letter from Madame Bienvenue to himself, no report at all? No, Mr. Chairman, I have not received the reports such as are indicated in the letter of Madame Bienvenue.

The minister received a letter signed Mrs. Bienvenue. He just accepts the resignation-oh, with a few kind words, "I wish to thank you very much for your contribution"-without making an inquiry to see if there is any truth in the letter. It did not occur to me, Mr. Chairman, that paragraph 4 had any relationship to the actual resignation incorporated

in the balance of the letter under the heading "Conclusions".

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I suggest, as there seems to be a good deal of interest in this item, that the minister could inquire of his colleague the Minister of Justice as to whether there were any reports such as alleged in paragraph 4 of the letter and of the sessional paper and the item might perhaps stand until the minister reports to the house. Before the item passes or is allowed to stand, Mr. Chairman, I should like to express the feeling of shock which I am sure must have been shared by other hon. members that the minister, having received this letter, accepted this resignation. The minister has, since he became minister, accepted more resignations than all the other members of the government put together, and yet he makes the statement that when he received this resignation he merely accepted it without investigating the circumstances which led up to it. Considering the importance of the positions held by many of the officials who have resigned since the minister took up his present office, it does seem to me the most extraordinary confession for the minister to make.

The hon. gentleman is not always accurate in his statements and on this occasion he is inaccurate. I said that I read the resignation and decided it had been made in good faith. I accepted it, but at no time did I say I had made no investigation, as the hon. member has now stated. In that respect his remarks are totally inaccurate and his gratuitous references to other

resignations deserve to be received with the contempt which one feels for that type of political remark.
Cheap.

The resignation of Mr. Mclvor from the Canadian wheat board was contemplated for many years, and was based upon personal reasons. The resignation of Mr. Bennett from the atomic energy commission had been placed before my predecessor at least one year before I assumed office and was very kindly postponed by Mr. Bennett at my request. So let us have no more of these snide remarks about resignations.
Hear, hear.

Before the hon. members assume that my observations should be treated with contempt I wish to say I have listened very carefully to the remarks of the minister. I certainly got the impression, as I believe did all members on this side of the house, that the minister had made no investigation of the case of Mrs. Bienvenue. If he made such an investigation would he tell us the results of it, which surely parliament is entitled to know.
I accept no responsibility for the impressions formed in the mind of my hon. friend.

The minister has said he made an investigation and that is a very pertinent statement in regard to the letter of Madame Bienvenue. As stated in this letter, and it must have been an important factor in the decision to resign, three reports were made, I rather assumed by the R.C.M.P. to the Minister of Justice from the reference to the R.C.M.P. in that paragraph. But perhaps that is wrong and perhaps the reports were made by someone else to the minister or to someone in his department. Now if the minister has made any investigation we would like to know whether as the result of such an investigation there was any foundation whatever for these serious charges that reports were made which reflected upon the character of Canadian personnel. If the minister is not in a position to give us the results of the investigation at this moment would he let this item stand until he is able to secure these results which he should be able to do quite shortly?

I think, Mr. Chairman, we are magnifying this item out of all reasonable proportion in asking for it to stand dependent upon a report from the Minister of Justice who was previously asked a question with regard to these reports. I have no
57071-3-155J
Supply-Trade and Commerce knowledge of reports which Madame Bienvenue claims are libellous or damaging to someone's reputation. This has not come to my attention in any way whatsoever and I have already stated the circumstances under which I have accepted the resignation.

Mr. Chairman, there is a very simple way out of this difficulty. The minister can ask an official of his department or someone else to phone the Minister of Justice to find out if he has any such reports. Agreed.

I think the item should pass. I think this is just a ridiculous request based on an alleged report said by Madame Bienvenue to be libellous. She does not say she saw the report; she simply says she heard of some report, but she does not tell us who was the author or to whom it was sent.
No, Mr. Chairman, it says she has learned of the reports.

Presumably in her capacity as the woman responsible for looking after the staff in Brussels. Supply-Trade and Commerce -hon. members opposite are very good at that-and I am sure the Minister of Justice will be quite able to give a reply on Monday.

The minister has now said that there were no such reports received by his department. I accept that statement. He did not make it earlier. I do not want to hold up the minister's estimates. At the proper time we will ask the Minister of Justice. Before the item carries, I should like to say this: the minister made a charge that I had misrepresented a statement he had made and in support of his contention that I had misrepresented him he went on to say that he had made an investigation. He has told us absolutely nothing about the kind of investigation he made or the results of his investigation, and I think that as representatives of the taxpayers we are entitled to that information before this item passes.

Before the item carries, I should like to ask the minister if he would be good enough to table the letters sent to him by the students, copies of which have, I think, also been sent to the Prime Minister.

There is a notice of motion on the order paper for a copy of all correspondence exchanged between the Prime Minister or the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the students who are acting as guides at the Canadian pavilion of the Brussels universal and international exhibition, 1958. That will come up in due course on Monday. The notice of motion refers to both the Prime Minister and myself. I have not had an opportunity of speaking to the Prime Minister about it.
Does the minister refuse to tell us what kind of investigation he carried out and what the results of his investigation were?
I see no purpose in attempting to satisfy the irrepressible curiosity of the hon. gentleman.

The charges made are public. They are public charges, and the documents have been tabled in this house. The minister says he has made an investigation. Can he not tell this committee what were the results of his investigation, what were his findings? Are the charges true or false?

Is the hon. member asking whether or not I investigated these charges made by Madame Bienvenue in paragraph

4 of her letter? I have already stated I have no knowledge of this whatsoever. If it were sent by the R.C.M.P., or to the Minister of Justice that is an entirely different proposition. In any case, her resignation is not founded on that statement in her letter but on considerations which do not even mention these alleged libelous charges.
I should like to ask one more question. Could the minister say what he investigated in the investigation he carried out?

Mr. Chairman, any reasonable person would understand what type of investigation would be carried out on receipt of a letter of resignation. I naturally asked my officials to let me know the state of affairs at Brussels.

And what did your officials report?
Churchill: My officials reported that Madame Bienvenue, in accordance with her letter was offering her resignation, that she was being asked to perform duties which were beyond her and was requesting more money, and they thought that this additional money was not available as it was not available within the estimate and no course was left other than to accept her resignation.

I am not going to press this matter any further. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I know that perhaps some of these questions are technical, but could the minister say, nevertheless, what are the bases upon which a licence is granted by his department for the export of power?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Can this power be recaptured? Is there a provision in the licence to this effect? What I mean is this: power is a natural resource and I am sure there must be conditions and terms upon which the licence is issued. Does the licence state that this power can be returned at any time and interrupted even though it may affect the development of communities in another country?

Yes, I believe so, because it is surplus power on our side and it is interruptible, and the communities receiving this on the other side do so on the understanding that they cannot count on it as a permanent thing.

Mr. Chairman, is there not a difference-and I speak subject to correction-between interruptible power and surplus power in the sense of power that is surplus to the immediate demands and which is provided on a more or less permanent basis? If this is interruptible power it could be interrupted at any time and if at the present moment there is no particular need for it in the province of New Brunswick there would not be much dispute about it on this side of the house. On the other hand, if it is power which is assumed to be in
Supply-Trade and Commerce excess of any immediately foreseeable requirement in New Brunswick and >s being exported to the state of Maine on a regular basis we would be very worried on this side of the house because in the last parliament, as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will probably recall, we were asked to support a loan of $30 million from the federal treasury to provide additional power for the province of New Brunswick and that measure received the support of both sides of the house. I do not think it would have received the support of both sides or indeed the support of a great many hon. members of the house if there had been any thought that in doing so we were making a loan to provide power for export to the United States.

Mr. Chairman, I think I can say it is genuinely interruptible power. It is making use of surplus power which is available at the present time but in the future it may well be that this surplus power will become essential for use within the province of New Brunswick itself.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I could get a more comprehensive answer to the question I asked earlier about the basis upon which these licences are granted. Supply-Trade and Commerce

speechtext: I know that the licences are granted in exceptional cases. I appreciate that they are not the general rule. What is required in order to recapture the power? Does notice have to be given to the industry or the power commission in the other state?

tell the committee if in such a permit there is a clause which determines the cost of power? In other words, is the power sold to the United States consumer at the same price that is paid for Canadian consumption by the residents of New Brunswick?

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to make an issue of anything and it may have been that way since the beginning of the world but when we were in another committee the other day I discovered that in terms of area the cities of Hull and Ottawa are linked together. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether there has been any change in the title of the bureau?
It is known as the dominion bureau of statistics.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I know but has there been any change in the title?

Mr. Chairman, in view of the very great interest in the compilation of unemployment statistics and, indeed, in view of the importance of these statistics at the present time, would the minister give the committee a fairly detailed report as to how this is done so that we may be in a position perhaps to appreciate more accurately than we have in the past the exact meaning and significance of the bureau of statistic's figures on unemployment compared with the figures collected by the Department of Labour.
An official from the bureau is coming down.

The reason I ask, and it should be obvious, is that there are two sets of figures as we all know and over the years there has been confusion inside and outside the house as to the relationship between the two and what they stand for, the registrations for unemployment assistance of the Department of Labour and the bureau of statistics sort of random sample compilation. The Leader of the Opposition has raised a question of very considerable importance because over the years some people have been a bit confused by the two sets of figures produced dealing with employment or unemployment. I believe that before my hon. friends altered their position this report was on the verge of being considered. It was brought to my attention last winter and because of other circumstances we did not have the opportunity then to give it the attention that it deserved. I have been considering asking Mr. Duffett, the head of the bureau, to bring the report forward again. I think that this report, based on his experience and that of his assistants might, if it meets with approval, solve this rather difficult problem. If my hon. friend will leave the matter there, I hope before very long to be able to report to him that we are making some progress along that line.

I appreciate what the minister has said and also the desirability, if it can be done, of consolidating the methods
Supply-Trade and Commerce and procedures and results of the efforts to clarify the situation with regard to unemployment and, indeed, employment statistics. If anything can be done in that regard, if a consolidation of that kind can be made, I am sure it will be very helpful. But in the meantime, as this is not likely to be accomplished for some time and two sets of reports will be coming out within the next few weeks, can the minister give the committee some indication of the basis of establishment that the bureau of statistics uses? It would surely be of value at this time if he could do that.
About 600 enumerators canvass 30,000 households every month and base their calculations upon their findings as they interview these households.

Then the basis is about 30,000 households in Canada. They are used as samples and on the basis of the information received from these 30,000 sample households across the country the figures that we get from the bureau of statistics on unemployment and employment are established?
I might add that it is based on the most modern scientific methods of making calculations from sampling.

The minister has now
occupied his present post for a year and during that year there has been a good deal of discussion of the question of employment and unemployment in various contexts. I assume he has satisfied himself that this is the best way to calculate employment and unemployment and that this is the most accurate reflection possible of the degree of employment and unemployment that we have in the country at this time.

This method of calculating employment has been in use for the last 13 years. It is the method available at the moment. I am not prepared to say that it is the best or that it might not be subject to improvement.

If I may pursue the matter for a moment, the minister will recall that when he and his friends were on this side of the house they disparaged these figures at all times and always used as unemployment figures the figures compiled by the unemployment insurance commission of the number of persons registered as looking for jobs. I take it from what the minister has said now that, since he moved across the house, he has changed his view and he now regards these figures as the proper figures to be used to reflect employment and unemployment.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
And the members opposite may in their turn adopt the other set of figures and, of course, the hon. member for Essex East has his own compilation which he gives to the house from time to time.

I might say that I have always been very scrupulous in using the figures given by the bureau of statistics in any public statements I have ever made, but I was anxious to find out whether the minister, who, with his friends, including his leader, was very critical of these figures when he sat over here, disparaged them at all times and suggested that they were more or less political figures, now has a different view of them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the minister explain the difference between the manner in which these figures are prepared or compiled and the manner in which the figures are prepared or compiled by the Department of Labour through the unemployment insurance commission?

They measure two different things. I think I answered a question along this line in the last parliament.
The second figure is based on our people who are registering for unemployment insurance. It is quite a different type of calculation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Nonetheless, the bureau of statistics comes out with both sets of figures, does it not?
It appears in a joint release from the dominion bureau of statistics.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: When are the figures released for each month? Is there a check date either at the beginning, the middle or end of the month on which this release is made?
Approximately in the third week of the month.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Following that up, why is it that in the course of the last several months, in a period of five or six months within the last twelve months, the figures were not available to members of parliament? I know that on several occasions questions were asked on orders of the day as to the reason for the delay. I am referring not only to the figures that are published by the minister's department but also to those that are compiled by unemployment insurance. I wondered why the delay did take place because I know that sometimes my release did not arrive in the third week of the month.

I know of no delay in the publication of these statistics by the dominion bureau of statistics. My hon. friend is referring also to those which come out from the

Department of Labour, and for which I have not any responsibility.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, I know the minister has no responsibility for them, but he said earlier that the bureau of statistics publishes both sets of figures in a joint statement. My complaint was that there had been delays in recent months.

Just to make it clear, when I said there had been no delay in the publication of this document by the dominion bureau of statistics I should have indicated quite clearly that was the joint release dealing with the two sets of figures.

speechtext: This is the third week of the month of July, and we have not yet received the figures for this month.
According to my book, the third week starts on the 21st, which is next week.
Surely the minister means the fourth week; three weeks have elapsed by the 21st. If you divide seven into 21, you get three.
The 1st of July was on a Tuesday, so I presume it will be out on Monday or Tuesday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does the minister know whether it will be out? Can an officer of the department say whether it will be out on Monday or Tuesday?
There is no fixed day or date and variations occur because of holidays and unforeseen events. But by and large, this report comes out sometime during the third week of each month.

I wonder if I might ask the minister to comment on a statement attributed to Mr. Gilbert Jackson in the Globe and Mail during last winter. I do not have the date, but I shall read a part of the statement:
I represented the 101,000 persons, in the first of these three categories-
That is the category he denotes as frictionally unemployed.
-as an almost irreducible minimum, even in the busiest season of the most prosperous year.
I want to know if, in fact, 100,000 is the figure of the irreducible minimum in that category as confirmed by the dominion bureau of statistics.

This question is a bit difficult because the 100,000-could that be related to a percentage of the total figure being considered-in relation to 500,000 would be quite different from relating it to a million or more.

The statement is that the figure of 100,000 represents an irreducible minimum even in the busiest season of the most prosperous year. There will be this number of persons between jobs or what is termed "frictionally unemployed".

There will be a number of people unemployed at certain times, people changing jobs or for other reasons. Whether or not you could categorically set that number of 100,000, is not information that we have available at this moment. I shall refer my hon. friend's question to the dominion bureau of statistics because it happens to be a very important inquiry into statistical surveys.

Board of grain commissioners-
406. Administration, $174,016.

Under the item for the board of grain commissioners I want to raise with the minister the question of an increase in the handling charges on grain being granted this year. The chairman of the board of grain commissioners, Mr. Roy Milner, has stated publicly that he expects a drive by the elevator companies to have the handling charges on grain increased. He says that one of the contributing factors is the likelihood of a light crop in certain areas. I rise to express the strongest possible objection to any increase in handling charges on grain being allowed this year.
I believe this is the most appropriate place to raise this question because, not only is the matter of handling charges within the jurisdiction of the board of grain commissioners, but following a judgment of the board of grain commissioners the government has the power to alter that decision. As a matter of fact, I think it goes even farther. I think the government has to approve the decision before it becomes effective. I base my objection to any increase in handling charges mainly on the ground that the prices to producers of wheat, oats, barley and other grains are already too low. It would be a very bad thing, therefore, for wheat producers if there were to be any further reduction in the prices at this time. I am not convinced that, from the standpoint of the elevator companies, they need an increase in rates or that they are justified in asking for an increase in handling charges. In travelling about western Canada one sees at the present time a whole rash of brand new elevators being constructed. When the country was opened up, elevators used to 57071-3-156
Supply-Trade and Commerce hold 25,000 bushels or 35,000 bushels of grain. Now the capacity has been doubled or tripled in comparison with that of the small elevators. These elevators, of course, are the property of the elevator companies but they are paid for either by the producers out of the proceeds that the producers would otherwise receive or directly from the national treasury through an item that is to be discussed a little later. This very rapid increase in elevator facilities, a very expensive expansion, is in my judgment an indication that the elevator companies are already making a sufficient profit at the current handling rate.
It helps unemployment.

I am all for helping unemployment. If you would pay some deficiency payments to the farmers, you would go even further in helping unemployment. I am going to deal with that matter a little later on. I hope the government will oppose an increase on tariffs on grain as it opposed the increase in freight rates in recent months. I hope the government will use the power it has to veto any increase that might be recommended; I hope the present chairman of the Canadian wheat board, Mr. W. C. McNamara, will follow the excellent precedent set for him by the former chairman of the wheat board Mr. George Mclvor who himself intervened, when an application was before the board of grain commissioners, to recommend against such an application being granted. I think the wheat board was wise, being the sole marketing agency for wheat and other grains, in the interests of producers to appear before the board of grain commissioners and to recommend against any increase in handling charges. I ask the minister what information he can give the committee on this point. From his appearance when I was making my remarks, I took it that he is opposed to an increase in handling charges. I am not endeavouring to misinterpret him at all. He has not said anything yet. We have to be careful these days.
I am in agreement with you for once.

I am glad to hear the minister say that. If he can now expand that a little and give us, and in particular the grain producers, the assurance that there will be no increase in handling charges, I am sure they will all thank him for his statement.

I am not going to go that far at this time until I receive a communication from the board of grain commissioners setting out all the facts in the case. But I am in agreement with the hon. member as to using every possible measure at our disposal within reason to keep costs down in

Supply-Trade and Commerce so far as our grain carrying charges are concerned and at the same time to increase the return to our producers.

I thank the minister for that statement. Knowing his usual frankness, I am quite sure that is ample assurance that there will be no increase in handling charges or that, if there is, the increase will not be taken from the pockets of the very hard-pressed grain producers.
I now come to the question of box car distribution which is a matter concurrently, I believe, in a legal way under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board. The Canadian wheat board, by means of shipping orders and by its contact with the railways, now allocates box cars amongst the elevator companies at the various railway points. The board of grain commissioners also has some jurisdiction in this field since the car order book provision is in the Canada Grain Act.
We have all been interested in the sittings of the Bracken royal commission on box car distribution and allocation. There was a report some weeks ago-which we were all sorry to read-that Mr. Bracken was not in the best of health and that he might be obliged to suspend for some time some of his activities in connection with this royal commisson. I am wonderng whether the minister can tell us at what stage the royal commission is now and when a report is likely to be received.
Before he does that, I want to say that the producers of western Canada have taken a tremendous interest in this royal commission. Whenever the royal commission has held public hearings at various places across western Canada there have been dozens of submissions and at most places where hearings were held hundreds of people appeared at those hearings. When the commission appeared at the city of Weyburn in my own constituency over 900 people came to the hearings. A few of them, of course, represented private elevator companies but by far the great majority of people at those hearings were producers themselves.
The producers are completely fed up with the system that now and for a number of years has forced them to deliver grain to any elevator that had space, whether or not they wished to patronize that elevator as a first choice. Another reason why so many people appeared before the royal commission, in my opinion, is the fact that grain producers are very much disturbed about the grain situation and are taking a more active interest in government policy in this regard than they have taken in many years. I think it is almost fantastic that, in a small city

like Weyburn, at one of these public hearings you would have many hundreds of grain producers appearing to suggest to the royal commission a fair system of box car allocation. I wonder whether the minister can say when the report is likely to be received and whether any action is likely to be taken on such report during the present session.

The inquiry being made into box cars and being conducted by Mr. Bracken has gone along very well indeed. I should like to reassure my hon. friend that Mr. Bracken is in good and vigorous health and has been pursuing his duties with that intense interest and attention that he always shows on matters of this kind on which he is particularly competent because he has conducted so many inquiries and investigations over the course of a long and active political career. It was at his suggestion that public hearings were held in the three prairie provinces so that farmers would have an opportunity of expressing their opinions concerning box car distribution. As has been pointed out, those meetings have been well attended and I think have proved to be very satisfactory. In other words, it meant that we were not doing something without the knowledge of the farmers as a whole and they have appreciated that fact very much. The inquiry is reaching a conclusion and Mr. Bracken informed me some days ago that he hoped to be able to report to me before the end of July.

I thank the minister for his statement. I am pleased to learn that Mr. Bracken is in good health and that his report will be made available to the minister by the end of July. I wonder whether the minister has any knowledge at this moment as to Mr. Bracken's recommendations even in a general way. I am wondering if he could tell the house whether or not action by parliament will be required during the current session on the assumption that his report is received by the end of this month.
I have no knowledge of what the report will contain. If action by parliament is required we will endeavour of course to take action immediately.

Mr. Chairman, there has been a good deal of interest in the matter of measuring and weighing grain. As the minister well knows, grain is now weighed on a bushel basis, the weight for wheat being 60 pounds to the bushel, and there is a growing belief that the unit should be changed to

a hundredweight. I am wondering if any action is contemplated in this regard at an early date. I may be conservative in this respect-
Hurrah.

I am sure the minister will accept my word when I say I am not sponsoring or promoting a mass delegation to Ottawa but I cannot help reading the newspapers and I have seen reports that farm organizations have scheduled August 1 as the last day until which they will wait for a reply from the government before taking action with respect to their mass delegation.
