I am hoping the answer will be favourable in spite of the many arguments raised even by the minister himself against deficiency payments, one of which was that it is difficult in Canada to provide deficiency payments since we are an exporting country and since most of the countries or all of the countries-I am not sure which way he put it-making deficiency payments are importers of wheat.
The minister knows that the United States is one of the major exporters of wheat and in some recent years when it has been the world's leading exporter of wheat it has paid from its national treasury a very substantial subsidy to grain producers. The figure as to the United States price for wheat contained in the Saskatchewan wheat pool brochure, which was printed in June of this year and which the minister has received, shows the United States set price to producers at $2.10 per bushel. It lists the various prices for wheat paid by many other countries, including the United Kingdom at $1.83, Austria at $2.50, Australia at $1.53, Belgium $2.50 and so on.
Canadian wheat producers received the lowest price paid to any wheat producers in a major wheat-producing country while, as the minister well knows, they operate in a very high-cost economy. Month by month their position steadily worsens and I am hoping the minister will announce a favourable decision by the government to make deficiency payments in line with the requests of farm organizations.
Some money is being paid from the national treasury into the wheat board account which in turn results in the price for wheat being maintained at a figure higher than would otherwise be the case. I know the producers are very grateful for the $4 million contained in the estimates, but I am sure if the government decided upon a deficiency payment it would have no trouble at all in selling it to other parts of Canada. I am quite certain that if the government announced such a deficiency payment on western grain there would not be a single

Supply-Trade and Commerce member on the government side who would voice any objection whatsoever. I am sure of that, although I am not too sure that the official opposition might not have one or two mavericks on this point because we know they had some in the past. I am positive, however, that the official position of the Liberal party would be in support and that that position would be supported by nearly all its members.
We in this group very strongly believe that agricultural producers, as all others, should be able to earn a living in keeping with the general Canadian standard, and I would ask the minister when he expects the government will arrive at this long-awaited decision. I can tell from the correspondence I am receiving and from people I have visited in recent weeks that there is great expectation in this regard in the three prairie provinces.
They are anxiously awaiting a government decision and I hope the minister can inform the house that a decision will be reached very shortly.

We had an exchange of opinion the other day on the subject of deficiency payments and I stated then that I hoped to be able to make an announcement in the course of a few days. At that time I inaccurately assumed the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce would be completed on Friday. I have lost, perhaps, a day and a half which might have been spent in grappling with this problem which loomed so large in the minds of a great many people.
I hope the threat of a mass movement on Ottawa scheduled for August 1 is nothing more than newspaper speculation, and I hope the responsible people in the prairie provinces in this period of grave international tension will not contemplate any such descent on Ottawa and the government. As I said the other night, we are dealing with this problem

it has a priority rating

and I suggested in the course of my remarks that a comprehensive farm program aimed at raising the income of western agriculturists might be of greater value than a large deficiency payment. However, I can assure the hon. member that it will not be many days before some announcement is made in accordance with the desire of so many people.
Now with regard to the item in the estimates dealing with wheat reserves, and the suggested $40 million put aside for that purpose, that, of course, is an estimate which might not be reached. It represents an increase over last year, and the increase results from an 11 million bushel storage

beyond the previous year because of new storage capacities and a shift in the proportion of oats and barley to wheat. It is also caused partly by increased carrying charges. The storage rate was raised to 1/30 of a cent per day, an increase of 12 per cent over the previous figure, and in the calculations which have been made it seemed wise to estimate for $40 million rather than $33 million. Of course, the carrying charges are paid on the excess quantity of wheat that the board has in storage beyond the 178 million bushels set out in the statute.

As I reported from time to time during the course of the last crop year the oats pool was in some difficulty. Barley was, too, for a while but recovered and, of course, we have done well with wheat. This item covers the deficit which was incurred in the oats pool and is another instance of governmental action in supporting prices. I believe that further consideration of this and the standing of various pools and the prospects for the future might be discussed when the members of the wheat board are here in two week's time.
